4.3.2 Urinary bladder
It is a median, pear shaped and distensible sac.
It is situated in the
pelvic region on the ventral side of the rectum in the abdomen.
It stores
300-800ml of urine temporarily which is brought by two ureters.
4.3.3 Urethra
It is a tube that takes urine from urinary bladder to outside.
The opening
of urinary bladder into urethra is guarded by a ring of muscles or sphincter.
Urethra is 4 cm long in females and open in to vestibule where as in males
it is about 20cm long.
Its opening is separate in females but is in common
with the reproductive tract in males (urino-genital duct).
4.4 Micturition
The urine is temporarily stored in the bladder.
There are two sets of
circular sphincter muscles in the bladder.
When the bladder is filling up,
both these sets of muscles are constricted, so the exit is closed.
However
as the pressure of the urine increases the walls of the bladder are stretched
and this triggers off an automatic reflex action which causes the upper
sphincter to relax.
But the lower sphincter is under the control of brain.
So urination is controlled.
Control of urination is not possessed by very
young children but is gradually learned.
Urinary bladder can store a maximum of 700-800 ml. of urine.
Urge
for micturition occurs when urinary bladder is filled with 300 - 400 ml. of
urine.
The stretched bladder stimulates nerve endings and sends signlas to
the brain.
At this time the urge becomes painful and leads to voluntary
micturition (release of urine from urinary bladder).
Total amount of urine
excreted per day is about 1.6-1.8 litres.
Its quantity increases with larger
intake of fluids like water, fruit juices and decreases with lesser intake.

4.5 Composition of urine
Urine is light yellowish fluid.
Urochrome formed by the breakdown
of haemoglobin in the blood is responsible for the yellowish colour of
urine.
It is a transparent fluid formed by urinary system.
Composition of
normal urine varies considerably depending on several factors.
For instance
taking a protein rich diet will results the formation of more urea in the
urine.
This is because the proteins get de-aminated in the liver with
subsequent formation of urea.
Even sugar can appear in a normal person
after a heavy intake of carbohydrates (sugars).
A large intake of liquids or
water - rich food increases the volume of water in the blood, hence more
often urine is excreted.
Urine contains 96% of water, 2.5% of organic substances (urea, uric
acid, creatine, creatinine, water soluble vitamins, hormones, and oxalates
etc) and 1.5% of inorganic solutes (sodium, chloride, phosphate, sulphate,
magnesium, calcium, iodine etc).
It is acidic (pH=6.0)in the beginning
but gradually becomes alkaline due to breakdown of urea to form ammonia.

Why do some people need to use a dialysis machine? Explain the principle involved in it

Required answer points

  • Dialysis is needed when both kidneys cannot adequately filter wastes
  • Blood is withdrawn and mixed with anticoagulant
  • Blood flows through a semipermeable membrane against dialysis fluid
  • Nitrogenous wastes diffuse out while cells/proteins are retained
  • Cleaned blood is returned

Optional answer points

  • Dialysis fluid resembles plasma but lacks nitrogenous waste

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • Dialysis permanently cures kidney failure

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

Some people need to use a dialysis machine because their kidneys are damaged or not functioning properly. The kidneys play a vital role in filtering waste products and excess fluids from the blood. When the kidneys are damaged, they cannot perform this function effectively, leading to the accumulation of poisonous wastes in the body, which can be life-threatening. Dialysis is a medical treatment that helps replace the function of the kidneys by filtering the blood.

4.6 Dialysis Machine (Artificial kidney)
Kidneys are vital organs for survival.
Several factors like infections, injury, very
high blood pressure, very high blood sugar
or restricted blood flow to kidneys leads to
accumulation of poisonous wastes in the
body and leads to death.
Dialysis machine is used to filter the
blood of a person when both kidneys are
damaged. The process is called
‘haemodialysis’. In this process, blood is taken out from the main artery,
mixed with an anticoagulant, such as heparin, and then pumped into the
apparatus called dialyzer. In this apparatus blood flows through channels
or tubes which are madeup of cellophane. These tubes are embedded in
the dialyzing fluid. A thin membrane separates the blood flowing inside
the tube and dialyzing fluid (dialysis), which has the same composition as
that of plasma, except the nitrogenous wastes.
As nitrogenous wastes are absent in dialyzing fluids, these substances
from the blood move out freely, there by cleaning the blood of its wastes.
This process is called "dialysis". This is similar to the function of the
kidney, but is different as there is no reabsorption involved .The cleaned
blood is pumped back to the body through a vein after adding anti-coagulant
(heparin). Each dialysis session lasts for 3 to 6 hours. This method has
been using for thousands of uremic / kidney failure patients all over the
world.

4.7 Kidney transplantation
The best long term solution for kidney failure (acute renal failure) is
Kidney transplantation. A functioning kidney is used in transplantation from
a donor preferably a close relative. The kidney that is received by a recipient
must be a good match to his body, to minimize the chances of rejection of
transplanted kidney by the immune system of the recipient. Modern clinical
procedures have increased the success rate of such complicated technique.

without any complications?

a lot for kidney failure patients. Organs are collected
from brain dead patients, then transplanted to the
recepient. This is called organ donation. To know
more about organ donation see in annexure.

but carry out excretion as a secondary function.
Lungs: In respiratory process lungs remove carbon dioxide and water

Some people need to use a dialysis machine when their kidneys are damaged and unable to filter waste products from the blood. This can happen due to infections, injury, high blood pressure, high blood sugar, or restricted blood flow to the kidneys, leading to the accumulation of poisonous wastes in the body, which can be fatal. The principle of a dialysis machine, also known as an artificial kidney, involves a process called 'haemodialysis.' In this process, blood is taken from the main artery and mixed with an anticoagulant to prevent clotting. It is then pumped into a device called a dialyzer. Inside the dialyzer, the blood flows through tubes made of cellophane, which are surrounded by a dialyzing fluid. This fluid has a similar composition to blood plasma but lacks nitrogenous wastes. A thin membrane separates the blood from the dialyzing fluid. Because the dialyzing fluid does not contain nitrogenous wastes, these wastes move from the blood into the fluid, effectively cleaning the blood. The cleaned blood is then returned to the body through a vein after adding an anticoagulant. Each dialysis session typically lasts between 3 to 6 hours. This process mimics the waste removal function of the kidneys but does not involve reabsorption of substances, which is a part of natural kidney function.

Some people need to use a dialysis machine because their kidneys are damaged and cannot properly filter waste products from their blood. The kidneys play a vital role in removing toxins, excess water, and other harmful substances from the body. When the kidneys fail to function, these wastes accumulate in the blood, leading to serious health issues and even death. Dialysis is a medical treatment that mimics the function of healthy kidneys by filtering the blood. The principle involved in dialysis is called 'haemodialysis'. In this process, blood is taken from the patient's artery, mixed with an anticoagulant to prevent clotting, and then passed through a dialyzer. The dialyzer contains a thin membrane that separates the blood from a dialyzing fluid. This fluid has a composition similar to plasma but lacks nitrogenous wastes. As a result, waste substances from the blood move into the dialyzing fluid, cleaning the blood. The cleaned blood is then returned to the patient's body through a vein. This process helps remove toxins and maintain the balance of water and electrolytes in the body.

The rhesus factor
There is another antigen of red blood cells which is present in 85% of the people of
Britain, this is known as the Rhesus factor, as it was first discovered in Rhesus monkeys.
People who have this are said to be Rhesus positive (Rh+).
Those who do not have this
factor are termed Rhesus negative (Rh-).
Normally they do not carry an antibody to this
factor in their plasma.
However, if Rh+ blood is transfused into the blood of a Rh- person,
against Rh-factors will be formed and these are capable of destroying Rh+ red cells.
Under
certain circumstances this is a potential hazard for babies.
If a Rh+ man marries a Rh- woman, some of the children are likely to be Rh+.
At birth
there is always some mixing of blood between the circulation of mother and baby and this
may occasionally happen during pregnancy.
So, if a child is Rh+ some of its blood will leak
into its mother’s circulation and cause antibodies to form in her blood.
If the mother has
more children, not all will necessarily be Rh+, but if they are, the amount of antibodies in
her blood often increases with each pregnancy, and in some instances the antibodies in her
blood may pass into the baby’s blood in sufficient quantities to produce very serious anaemia
and even death.
Fortunately these cases are not frequent, and when they do occur, the baby
is given a complete transfusion soon after birth so that the baby’s blood is replaced by
blood containing no antibodies to the rhesus factor.
It is now possible for this transfusion
to be carrried out before birth.
Another recently developed technique is for the mother to
be given an injection shortly after the birth of her first child which prevents the Rh+ cells
from stimulating the production of the harmful antibody.

Britain, this is known as the Rhesus factor, as it was first discovered in Rhesus monkeys.
People who have this are said to be Rhesus positive (Rh+).
Those who do not have this
factor are termed Rhesus negative (Rh-).
Normally they do not carry an antibody to this
factor in their plasma.
However, if Rh+ blood is transfused into the blood of a Rh- person,
against Rh-factors will be formed and these are capable of destroying Rh+ red cells.
Under
certain circumstances this is a potential hazard for babies.
If a Rh+ man marries a Rh- woman, some of the children are likely to be Rh+.
At birth
there is always some mixing of blood between the circulation of mother and baby and this
may occasionally happen during pregnancy.
So, if a child is Rh+ some of its blood will leak
into its mother’s circulation and cause antibodies to form in her blood.
If the mother has
more children, not all will necessarily be Rh+, but if they are, the amount of antibodies in
her blood often increases with each pregnancy, and in some instances the antibodies in her
blood may pass into the baby’s blood in sufficient quantities to produce very serious anaemia
and even death.
Fortunately these cases are not frequent, and when they do occur, the baby
is given a complete transfusion soon after birth so that the baby’s blood is replaced by
blood containing no antibodies to the rhesus factor.
It is now possible for this transfusion
to be carrried out before birth.
Another recently developed technique is for the mother to
be given an injection shortly after the birth of her first child which prevents the Rh+ cells
from stimulating the production of the harmful antibody.

4.6 Dialysis Machine (Artificial kidney)
Kidneys are vital organs for survival.
Several factors like infections, injury, very
high blood pressure, very high blood sugar
or restricted blood flow to kidneys leads to
accumulation of poisonous wastes in the
body and leads to death.
Dialysis machine is used to filter the
blood of a person when both kidneys are
damaged.
The process is called
‘haemodialysis’.
In this process, blood is taken out from the main artery,
mixed with an anticoagulant, such as heparin, and then pumped into the
apparatus called dialyzer.
In this apparatus blood flows through channels
or tubes which are madeup of cellophane.
These tubes are embedded in
the dialyzing fluid.
A thin membrane separates the blood flowing inside
the tube and dialyzing fluid (dialysis), which has the same composition as
that of plasma, except the nitrogenous wastes.
As nitrogenous wastes are absent in dialyzing fluids, these substances
from the blood move out freely, there by cleaning the blood of its wastes.
This process is called "dialysis".
This is similar to the function of the
kidney, but is different as there is no reabsorption involved .The cleaned
blood is pumped back to the body through a vein after adding anti-coagulant
(heparin).
Each dialysis session lasts for 3 to 6 hours.
This method has
been using for thousands of uremic / kidney failure patients all over the
world.

4.7 Kidney transplantation
The best long term solution for kidney failure (acute renal failure) is
Kidney transplantation.
A functioning kidney is used in transplantation from
a donor preferably a close relative.
The kidney that is received by a recipient
must be a good match to his body, to minimize the chances of rejection of
transplanted kidney by the immune system of the recipient.
Modern clinical
procedures have increased the success rate of such complicated technique.

This is called organ donation.

Lungs, skin, liver and large intestine have their own specific functions

Lungs: In respiratory process lungs remove carbon dioxide and water
vapour.
Skin: It consists of large number of sweat glands richly supplied with
blood capillaries, from which they extract sweat and some metabolic
wastes from blood.
Since the skin sends out plenty of water and small
amount of salts in the form of sweat.
It serves as an accessory excretory
organ.

How does phototropism occur in plants?

Required answer points

  • Phototropism is directional growth in response to light
  • The shoot tip perceives lateral light
  • Auxin influence is redistributed to the shaded side
  • Greater elongation on the shaded side bends the shoot toward light

Optional answer points

  • Reference Darwin/Went coleoptile experiments

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • Light destroys every auxin molecule on the lit side

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

Phototropism in plants occurs when the plant bends towards light. Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin conducted experiments where they covered the tip of a seedling's stem (coleoptile) with a metal foil cylinder. When exposed to light from the side, the seedling did not bend, but when light could reach the tip, it bent normally. This suggested that some 'influence' was transmitted from the upper part to the lower part of the stem, causing it to bend. In 1926, F.W. Went discovered that this 'influence' was a chemical stimulus called auxin. Auxin, a plant hormone, is responsible for the bending of the stem towards light. This type of response to light is called phototropism.

118Government’s Gift for Students’ Progress Coordination
Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin performed some
experiments on phototropism. They covered the terminal portion of the
tip of stem(coleoptile) with a cylinder of metal foil. Exposed the plant to
light coming from the side. The characteristic bending of the seedling did
not occur. When, light was permitted to penetrate the cylinder, bending of
the seedling occurred normally. They stated that when seedlings are freely
exposed to a lateral light some ‘influence’ is transmitted from upper to
the lower part causing the material to bend.
In 1926, the Dutch plant physiologist F.W. Went succeeded in
separating this ‘influence’ responsible for bending from the plant that
produced it. Went cut-off coleoptile tips from oat
seedlings. He placed the tips on a slice of agar and left
them for about an hour. He then cut the agar into small
blocks and placed a block on one side of stump of the
decapitated seedlings. They were kept in the dark during
the entire experiment. Within one hour he observed a
distinct bending away from the side on which the agar
block was placed.
Agar block that had not been in contact with coleoptile tip produced
either no bending or only a slight bending toward the side on which the
block had been placed.
Went interpreted these experiments as showing that the coleoptile tip
exerted its effect by means of chemical stimulus rather than a physical
stimulus such as an electrical impulse. This chemical stimulus came to be
known as auxin. In this way the first plant hormone auxin (greek word
auxin means to increase) was discovered by Went.
5.14 Tropic and nastic movements in plants
The above experiments show that movement of individual parts of plants
is possible when they are subjected to external stimuli. This type of
response is called tropism or tropic movement. Sometimes the direction
of stimuli determines direction of movement, sometimes
the direction of movement may not be determined by
direction of stimuli. This type of response is called nastic
movement.
Let us observe the growth of a creeper plant near
window. The shoots of creeper bend towards sunlight.

Such type of response of a plant to light is called phototropism (photo
means light, tropism means movement).
We know that roots always grow downwards. This means that plant
respond positively for gravitational force. This is called geotropism.
If we observe plant which grow near a rock or wall side. You notice
that all roots are growing in one direction, away from the rock or wall
where water is available in the soil. This type of response to water is called
hydrotropism.
A very interesting thing in plants is movement of tendrils. All plants
show positive response to phototropism. But in creepers like cucumber,
bitter gourd, the stem is weak and thin. Hence plant cannot grow erect.
Tendrils play a vital role to make the plant erect. Tendrils are thin thread
like growths on the leaves or stems of climbing plant. They grow towards
support and wind around them. This type of response to make contact or
touch is called "thigmotropism".
If you taste the carpel of a flower it is sweet. Let us recall butterflies
fluttering on flowers for the nectar. Ripen stigma secretes sugary substance.
This chemical substance stimulates the pollen grain which falls on the
stigma. Pollen grain responds to this stimulus and germinate to produce
pollen tubes to reach the ovule for fertilization. This type of response to
chemicals is called "chemotropism." Unequal distribution of auxins affects
the root and the stem growth. High concentration of auxin stimulates stem
growth and inhibit root growth.

gold

Phototropism in plants occurs when they respond to light by bending towards it. This process was studied by Charles Darwin and his son, who found that when the tip of a plant's stem (coleoptile) is covered and exposed to light from one side, the plant does not bend. However, if light is allowed to reach the tip, the plant bends towards the light. This indicates that some 'influence' is transmitted from the tip to the lower parts of the plant, causing it to bend. F.W. Went later identified this 'influence' as a chemical stimulus, which he named auxin. He demonstrated that when the coleoptile tips were placed on agar blocks and then applied to one side of a decapitated seedling, the seedling bent away from the side with the agar block. This showed that auxin, a plant hormone, is responsible for the bending by promoting growth on one side of the plant, causing it to bend towards the light source. Thus, phototropism is a result of the uneven distribution of auxin in response to light, leading to differential growth and bending towards the light.

Local Qwen — Retrieved evidence

Phototropism in plants occurs when the plant bends towards a light source. This response is due to the plant's ability to sense light and the distribution of a chemical called auxin. When light hits one side of the plant, more auxin accumulates on the shaded side. Auxin causes the cells on the shaded side to grow faster, making the plant bend towards the light. This was demonstrated by Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin, who found that the tip of the plant (coleoptile) is responsible for sensing light. Further experiments by F.W. Went showed that the bending is caused by a chemical stimulus, which is now known as auxin. The auxin is produced in the tip of the plant and moves down to the stem, causing the cells on the shaded side to elongate more, leading to the bending of the stem towards the light.

a membranous structure, consisting of 3
membranes.
The inner most layer forms

It is believed to be a site for trapping of

portion is called as stroma.
It is believed to
be responsible for enzymatic reactions
leading to the synthesis of glucose, which
in turn join together to form starch.
Substances found in chloroplast which capture sunlight are called
photosynthetic pigments.
There are several types of photosynthetic
pigments involved in the process to produce organic molecules like
glucose in plants.
Chlorophyll is such a pigment which contain one atom of magnesium.
It is similar in structure to the haem of haemoglobin (The iron containing
red pigment that transports oxygen in blood.).
Two major kinds of chlorophylls are associated with thylakoid
membranes.
Chlorophyll ‘a’ is bluish-green in colour and chlorophyll ‘b’
is yellowish-green colour.
Around 250 to 400 pigment molecules are
grouped as light harvesting complex or photosynthetic unit in each

green plants in the process of photosynthesis.

Nutrition 12
1.3 Mechanism of Photosynthesis
1.3.1 Light dependent reaction (Light phase)
In this reaction light plays a key role.
A series of chemical reactions
occur in a very quick succession initiated by light and therefore the phase
is technically called the photochemical phase or light dependent reaction.
The light reaction takes place in chlorophyll containing thylakoids called
grana of chloroplasts.
Several steps occur in the light dependent reaction.
Step-I : The chlorophyll on exposure to light energy becomes activated
by absorbing photons. (Photon is a unit of light energy)
Step-II: This energy is used in splitting water molecule to release O2.
This reaction is known as photolysis (photo means light, lysis
means breaking).
This was discovered by Robert Hill.
Hence it
is also called Hill’s reaction.
Hydrogen produced in photolysis is immediately picked up by special
compound NADP (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide Phosphate) to form
NADPH (Reduced NADP).
Another energy rich compound A TP
(Adenosine triphosphate) is also formed at the end of the light reaction.
1.3.2 Light independent reaction (Dark phase)
This reaction does not require the presence of light and extension of
the phases after day time may occur in some plants.
This is also called
dark reaction.
But the term dark reaction does not mean that it occurs
when it is dark at night.
It only means that these reactions do not depend
on light.
It takes place in stroma of chloroplast.
In the dark phase the
hydrogen combines with CO2 by utilizing A TP energy and produces glucose
(C6H12O6).
This synthesis occurs in a number of steps using certain special
intermediate compounds and enzymes.
Finally glucose may be converted
into storage product starch.
Plants are capable of surviving under a range of situations, from very
hot, dry and bright light conditions to wet, humid and dim light condition.
The requirement of light and other factors varies from one plant to another.

1.4.1 How do organisms obtain their nutrition?
Depending on the type and availability of food organisms
can adapt to a range of strategies of food intake and use.
Some organisms like bread mold, yeast, mushrooms etc.
break down the food materials outside the body and then absorb
it.
They are called as saprophytes.
Some other organisms
derive nutrition from plants or animals without killing them.
This type of parasitic nutritive strategy is used by a wide variety
of organisms like Cuscuta, lice, leeches and tape worms.
Others
take in whole material and break it down inside their bodies.
Intake and braking down of food depends on the bodys’ structure
and it’s function.
Since the food and the way it is obtained differs, the
digestive system is also different in various organisms.
In single
celled organisms, like Amoeba the food may be taken in by
the entire surface but as the complexity of the organism
increases, different parts become specialized to perform
different functions.
For example Amoeba as shown in Fig-9(a)
it takes in food using temporary finger like extensions
(pseudopodia) of the cell surface which fuse over the food
particle forming food vacuole.

118 Coordination
Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin performed some
experiments on phototropism.
They covered the terminal portion of the
tip of stem(coleoptile) with a cylinder of metal foil.
Exposed the plant to
light coming from the side.
The characteristic bending of the seedling did
not occur.
When, light was permitted to penetrate the cylinder, bending of
the seedling occurred normally.
They stated that when seedlings are freely
exposed to a lateral light some ‘influence’ is transmitted from upper to
the lower part causing the material to bend.
In 1926, the Dutch plant physiologist F.W.
Went succeeded in
separating this ‘influence’ responsible for bending from the plant that
produced it.
Went cut-off coleoptile tips from oat
seedlings.
He placed the tips on a slice of agar and left
them for about an hour.
He then cut the agar into small
blocks and placed a block on one side of stump of the
decapitated seedlings.
They were kept in the dark during
the entire experiment.
Within one hour he observed a
distinct bending away from the side on which the agar
block was placed.
Agar block that had not been in contact with coleoptile tip produced
either no bending or only a slight bending toward the side on which the
block had been placed.
Went interpreted these experiments as showing that the coleoptile tip
exerted its effect by means of chemical stimulus rather than a physical
stimulus such as an electrical impulse.
This chemical stimulus came to be
known as auxin.
In this way the first plant hormone auxin (greek word
auxin means to increase) was discovered by Went.
5.14 Tropic and nastic movements in plants
The above experiments show that movement of individual parts of plants
is possible when they are subjected to external stimuli.
This type of
response is called tropism or tropic movement.
Sometimes the direction
of stimuli determines direction of movement, sometimes
the direction of movement may not be determined by
direction of stimuli.
This type of response is called nastic
movement.
Let us observe the growth of a creeper plant near
window.
The shoots of creeper bend towards sunlight.

retrieved

Phototropism in plants is the growth movement in response to light. This process is primarily controlled by plant hormones called auxins. When a plant is exposed to light from one direction, auxins accumulate on the shaded side of the plant. This causes the cells on that side to elongate more than those on the side exposed to light, resulting in the bending of the plant towards the light source. This bending allows the plant to maximize its exposure to sunlight, which is essential for photosynthesis. The experiments by Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin demonstrated that the tip of the plant is crucial for sensing light and directing growth, as covering the tip prevented the bending response. Later, F.W. Went identified auxin as the chemical responsible for this growth response, confirming that it acts as a chemical stimulus rather than a physical one.

118 Coordination
Charles Darwin and his son Francis Darwin performed some
experiments on phototropism.
They covered the terminal portion of the
tip of stem(coleoptile) with a cylinder of metal foil.
Exposed the plant to
light coming from the side.
The characteristic bending of the seedling did
not occur.
When, light was permitted to penetrate the cylinder, bending of
the seedling occurred normally.
They stated that when seedlings are freely
exposed to a lateral light some ‘influence’ is transmitted from upper to
the lower part causing the material to bend.
In 1926, the Dutch plant physiologist F.W.
Went succeeded in
separating this ‘influence’ responsible for bending from the plant that
produced it.
Went cut-off coleoptile tips from oat
seedlings.
He placed the tips on a slice of agar and left
them for about an hour.
He then cut the agar into small
blocks and placed a block on one side of stump of the
decapitated seedlings.
They were kept in the dark during
the entire experiment.
Within one hour he observed a
distinct bending away from the side on which the agar
block was placed.
Agar block that had not been in contact with coleoptile tip produced
either no bending or only a slight bending toward the side on which the
block had been placed.
Went interpreted these experiments as showing that the coleoptile tip
exerted its effect by means of chemical stimulus rather than a physical
stimulus such as an electrical impulse.
This chemical stimulus came to be
known as auxin.
In this way the first plant hormone auxin (greek word
auxin means to increase) was discovered by Went.
5.14 Tropic and nastic movements in plants
The above experiments show that movement of individual parts of plants
is possible when they are subjected to external stimuli.
This type of
response is called tropism or tropic movement.
Sometimes the direction
of stimuli determines direction of movement, sometimes
the direction of movement may not be determined by
direction of stimuli.
This type of response is called nastic
movement.
Let us observe the growth of a creeper plant near
window.
The shoots of creeper bend towards sunlight.

10 GEN-BIO-010

What is a synapse, and how does it transfer information?

Required answer points

  • A synapse is the functional contact region between two neurons
  • The neurons are separated by a minute gap without protoplasmic continuity
  • Signals cross chemically, electrically, or both

Optional answer points

  • Synapses are common in the brain and spinal cord

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • The cytoplasm of the two neurons is continuous

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

A synapse is the functional region where two nerve cells (neurons) communicate. It is a tiny gap between the dendrites of one neuron and the axon of another neuron. Information is transferred across the synapse through chemical or electrical signals. The synapse allows the transmission of information from one neuron to another, enabling communication within the nervous system.

Synapse
Synapse is the functional region of contact
between two neurons, where information from one
neuron is transmitted or relayed to another neuron.

essentially neurons do not have any protoplasmic
connection between them yet information is passed
from one nerve cell to the other through these gaps
either in the form of chemical or electrical signals
or both. These synapses are mainly found usually in
the brain, spinal cord and around the spinal cord.
Beyond these areas the axon carries the signals
from brain and spinal cord to respective parts of
our body.

A synapse is the functional region of contact between two neurons. It is where information from one neuron is transmitted or relayed to another neuron. Although there are minute gaps between neurons at the synapse, and they do not have any direct protoplasmic connection, information is still passed through these gaps. This transmission occurs in the form of chemical or electrical signals, or both. Synapses are mainly found in the brain, spinal cord, and around the spinal cord, facilitating communication within the nervous system.

100 Coordination
Everyday we do many activities such as sharpening of a pencil, grasping
a door knob, walking or running, driving, and a few physical actions.
All
these actions involve well coordinated movements made with well balanced
postures.
In fact, whenever we move some basic functions such as
movement, balance and coordination work together in performing motions
of body parts.
Even standing upright is a challenge of balancing on just two feet with
a narrow base.
Yet, it is common for us not only to stand upright easily and
apparently, effortlessly, but also while keeping our balance to perform
many functions like walking, running etc.
x What other functions do you think are needed in coordination and
balance?
All our functions are carried out by an effort of several systems
working together.
For example, while movement, we hardly ever use just
the skeletal system or muscular system alone, several other systems also
have their own roles to play.
Even within the muscular system, several
muscles work in a systamatic manner.
x What triggers the movement of the muscles?
All our body parts, mainly the tissues and cells in them work by picking
up signals of change (also called as stimuli) from their surroundings.
They
then respond to them.
This process triggers different functions in our body.
For example, it is natural to move to a side of the road when we hear or see
a car approaching.

5.1 Responding to stimuli
x What helps us to respond to such signals of change?
x Why does the living body respond to such signals?
All living organisms respond to stimuli.
Changes in the surroundings
or signals of changes or stimulus are reasons for responses by living
organisms.
The cat may be running because it saw a mouse.
Plants grow
towards the sunlight.
We start sweating when the surroundings are hot and
humid.
The ability to react to particular stimulus in a particular situation
must be of great importance in ensuring the survival of the organism.
There is a sequence of events that brings about responses.
They start
from detecting a change in outer or inner environment of the body or
stimuli, then transmission of the information is the second stage, processing
of the same is the third stage and execution of the appropriate action is
last stage.

5.4 Pathways: From stimulus to response
In the holding stick activity you observed that there is coordination
between eye and fingers.
Different pathways are taken by nerves to bring
about this coordinated activity.
On the basis of pathways followed, nerves are classified mainly into
three different types.
They are as follows.
(A) Afferent nerves or Sensory nerves :
The nerves which carry messages towards the central nervous system
(spinal cord or brain) from nerve endings on the muscles of different sense
organs are called afferent or sensory nerves.
(B) Efferent nerves or motor nerves :
The nerves which carry messages from the central nervous system to
body parts that shall carry out the response to effector muscles are called
efferent or motor nerves.
(C) Association nerves (Interneurons) :
These nerves link together the afferent and efferent nerves in central
nervous system (brain and spinal cord).

Knee jerk reflex
Cross the legs, in a seated position, so that the lower
half of the uppermost leg hangs freely over the other.
Strike
the area below the knee cap sharply with a rubber hammer,

Such a response is said to be involuntary reflexes.

the same thigh muscle can operate in a voluntary manner,

A synapse is the functional region of contact between two neurons. It is where information from one neuron is transmitted to another. Although there is a minute gap between neurons at the synapse, information is passed through these gaps in the form of chemical or electrical signals, or both. This process allows neurons to communicate effectively, enabling the transmission of signals throughout the nervous system. Synapses are primarily found in the brain and spinal cord, facilitating complex processes like thought, movement, and reflexes.

100 Coordination
Everyday we do many activities such as sharpening of a pencil, grasping
a door knob, walking or running, driving, and a few physical actions.
All
these actions involve well coordinated movements made with well balanced
postures.
In fact, whenever we move some basic functions such as
movement, balance and coordination work together in performing motions
of body parts.
Even standing upright is a challenge of balancing on just two feet with
a narrow base.
Yet, it is common for us not only to stand upright easily and
apparently, effortlessly, but also while keeping our balance to perform
many functions like walking, running etc.
x What other functions do you think are needed in coordination and
balance?
All our functions are carried out by an effort of several systems
working together.
For example, while movement, we hardly ever use just
the skeletal system or muscular system alone, several other systems also
have their own roles to play.
Even within the muscular system, several
muscles work in a systamatic manner.
x What triggers the movement of the muscles?
All our body parts, mainly the tissues and cells in them work by picking
up signals of change (also called as stimuli) from their surroundings.
They
then respond to them.
This process triggers different functions in our body.
For example, it is natural to move to a side of the road when we hear or see
a car approaching.

Synapse
Synapse is the functional region of contact
between two neurons, where information from one
neuron is transmitted or relayed to another neuron.
Though these are regions of minute gaps and
essentially neurons do not have any protoplasmic
connection between them yet information is passed
from one nerve cell to the other through these gaps
either in the form of chemical or electrical signals
or both.
These synapses are mainly found usually in
the brain, spinal cord and around the spinal cord.
Beyond these areas the axon carries the signals
from brain and spinal cord to respective parts of
our body.
104 Coordination
5.4 Pathways: From stimulus to response
In the holding stick activity you observed that there is coordination
between eye and fingers.
Different pathways are taken by nerves to bring
about this coordinated activity.
On the basis of pathways followed, nerves are classified mainly into
three different types.
They are as follows.
(A) Afferent nerves or Sensory nerves :
The nerves which carry messages towards the central nervous system
(spinal cord or brain) from nerve endings on the muscles of different sense
organs are called afferent or sensory nerves.
(B) Efferent nerves or motor nerves :
The nerves which carry messages from the central nervous system to
body parts that shall carry out the response to effector muscles are called
efferent or motor nerves.
(C) Association nerves (Interneurons) :
These nerves link together the afferent and efferent nerves in central
nervous system (brain and spinal cord).

Knee jerk reflex
Cross the legs, in a seated position, so that the lower

11 GEN-BIO-011

Why do fish and frog produce a huge number of eggs each year?

Required answer points

  • Fertilisation is external in water
  • Eggs and sperm are exposed to currents and predators
  • The chance of any one gamete/egg surviving and being fertilised is low
  • Large numbers compensate for high loss

Optional answer points

  • No parental protection is available for many eggs

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • Every released egg is fertilised

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

Fish and frogs produce a huge number of eggs each year because they undergo external fertilization. In this process, the eggs are laid in water, and the male releases a large number of sperms to increase the chances of fertilization. Since external fertilization is dependent on natural factors like water currents and the presence of the female, the chances of successful fertilization are low. To compensate for this, a vast number of eggs and sperms are produced to ensure that at least some eggs get fertilized and develop into offspring.

6.4 Sexual reproduction
As you have studied earlier, sexual reproduction is a method of
reproduction where fusion of gametes takes place, by a process called
fertilization. Fertilization may occur either outside the body of the female
organism (external fertilization) or inside the female’s body (internal
fertilization). As a matter of fact, in land animals like mammals the eggs are
fertilised inside the body of female organism. The fertilized egg (the zygote)
start dividing and grow into the embryo.
External fertilization is observed in aquatic animals like most of the fishes
and amphibians. The female lays a vast number of eggs in water and male
animal release some millions of sperms on them. As the chance of fertilization
is controlled by nature which occurs externally, hence it is inevitable to
produce a vast number of eggs and sperms.
6.5 Reproduction in placental mammals - Human beings
While talking about placental mammals especially human beings special
reproductive organs have developed in males and females to carry out
reproduction. Let us study them in detail.
6.6 Male reproductive system
Observe the Fig-13(a) of male
reproductive system and findout the parts. (1)
a pair of testes, (2) a pair of vasa efferentia, (3)
a pair of epididymis, (4) a pair of vasa
deferentia, (5) a pair of seminal vesicles, (6) a
pair of ejaculatory ducts, (7) prostate gland,
(8) a pair of cowper’s gland, (9) urethra. Let us
known their arrangement and functions.
Testes : The testes are located outside the
abdominal cavity within a pouch called scrotum.
In each testis highly coiled seminiferous
tubules are present. The sperms are produced
in these tubules by meiosis in very large numbers (hundreds of millions).
Male sex hormone testosterone is also produced in testes.
x Think why testes are located outside the abdominal cavity?
The scrotum helps in maintaining low temperature of the testes
(2 to 2.5o C lower than the body temperature) necessary for sperm formation.

Vasa efferentia : The seminiferous tubules open into vasa efferentia. They
carry sperms into the epididymis.
Epididymis : One in each side, the vasa efferentia open into epididymis
which is a highly coiled tube located along the posterior side of testes.
Sperms are stored in them.
Vasa deferentia : From each epididymis arises vas deferens which ascends
into the abdominal cavity looping around the ureter.
Seminal vesicles : They open into the vas deferens. They produce seminal
fluid. It is the source of energy for sperms when they are outside the body.
Prostrate gland: The main function of the prostrate gland is to secrete
prostrate fluid which is one of the component of semen supplies nutrients
to the sperm.
Cowper’s gland : Secretions of these glands help to neutralise the acidity
in the walls of urethra and the free flow of the sperm cells
Ejaculatory duct : A duct from seminal vesicles joins the vas deferens and
continues as ejaculatory duct. Two ejaculatory ducts join at the centre of
urethra.
Urethra : In males it transports not only urine but also sperms. It is also
called as urino-genital duct.

female nucleus during fertilisation.
Head and middle piece are attached by neck. Mitochondria of

Fish and frogs produce a huge number of eggs each year because they undergo external fertilization. In this process, the female lays a large number of eggs in water, and the male releases millions of sperms over them. Since fertilization occurs outside the body and is controlled by natural conditions, producing a vast number of eggs and sperms increases the chances of successful fertilization.

6.4 Sexual reproduction
As you have studied earlier, sexual reproduction is a method of
reproduction where fusion of gametes takes place, by a process called
fertilization. Fertilization may occur either outside the body of the female
organism (external fertilization) or inside the female’s body (internal
fertilization). As a matter of fact, in land animals like mammals the eggs are
fertilised inside the body of female organism. The fertilized egg (the zygote)
start dividing and grow into the embryo.
External fertilization is observed in aquatic animals like most of the fishes
and amphibians. The female lays a vast number of eggs in water and male
animal release some millions of sperms on them. As the chance of fertilization
is controlled by nature which occurs externally, hence it is inevitable to
produce a vast number of eggs and sperms.
6.5 Reproduction in placental mammals - Human beings
While talking about placental mammals especially human beings special
reproductive organs have developed in males and females to carry out
reproduction. Let us study them in detail.
6.6 Male reproductive system
Observe the Fig-13(a) of male
reproductive system and findout the parts. (1)
a pair of testes, (2) a pair of vasa efferentia, (3)
a pair of epididymis, (4) a pair of vasa
deferentia, (5) a pair of seminal vesicles, (6) a
pair of ejaculatory ducts, (7) prostate gland,
(8) a pair of cowper’s gland, (9) urethra. Let us
known their arrangement and functions.
Testes : The testes are located outside the
abdominal cavity within a pouch called scrotum.
In each testis highly coiled seminiferous
tubules are present. The sperms are produced
in these tubules by meiosis in very large numbers (hundreds of millions).
Male sex hormone testosterone is also produced in testes.

Reflection of light at curved surfacesReproduction131Government’s Gift for Students’ Progress
Vasa efferentia : The seminiferous tubules open into vasa efferentia. They
carry sperms into the epididymis.
Epididymis : One in each side, the vasa efferentia open into epididymis
which is a highly coiled tube located along the posterior side of testes.
Sperms are stored in them.
Vasa deferentia : From each epididymis arises vas deferens which ascends
into the abdominal cavity looping around the ureter.
Seminal vesicles : They open into the vas deferens. They produce seminal
fluid. It is the source of energy for sperms when they are outside the body.
Prostrate gland: The main function of the prostrate gland is to secrete
prostrate fluid which is one of the component of semen supplies nutrients
to the sperm.
Cowper’s gland : Secretions of these glands help to neutralise the acidity
in the walls of urethra and the free flow of the sperm cells
Ejaculatory duct : A duct from seminal vesicles joins the vas deferens and
continues as ejaculatory duct. Two ejaculatory ducts join at the centre of
urethra.
Urethra : In males it transports not only urine but also sperms. It is also
called as urino-genital duct.

Head and middle piece are attached by neck. Mitochondria of
middle piece produce energy for the movement of the sperm. The
tail propels the sperm.

2.8 Evolution in gases exchanging system
Exchange of gases is a common life process in all living organisms,
but it is not same in all.
Single celled organisms Amoeba or multicellular
organisms like Hydra, Planaria, roundworms and earthworms obtain
oxygen and expel carbon dioxide directly from the body by the process of
diffusion.
In other multicellular animals special organs are evolved.
Animals
either terrestrial or aquatic adapted to different types of respiration and
possess different types of respiratory organs mostly depending on the
habitat in which they live.
Body size, availability of water and the type of
their circulatory system are some of the factors for the animals to develop
different types of respiratory organs.
There is tracheal respiratory system in insects like cockroach,
grasshopper etc.
Tracheal respiratory system consists of series of tubes
called trachea.
This is divided into fine branches called tracheoles which
carry air directly to the cells in the tissues.
Some aquatic animals like fishes have developed special organs for
respiration which are known as gills or branchiae.
Blood supplied to gills
through capillaries which have thin walls where gases are exchanged.
This
is called branchial respiration (gill respiration).
Fish keeps its mouth open
and lowers the floor of the oral cavity.
As a result water from outside will
be drawn into the oral cavity.
Now the mouth is closed and the floor of the
oral cavity is raised.
Water is pushed into the pharynx and is forced to gill
pouches through internal branchial apertures.
Gill lamellae are bathed with
water and absorbs the oxygen dissolved in the water.

Respiration through skin is called cutaneous respiration.
Frog an
amphibian can respire through cutaneous and pulmonary respiration
(through lungs) processes as well as Bucco-Pharyngeal Cavity.
Terrestrial
animals like reptiles, birds and mammals, respire through lungs.

2.9 Respiration in Plants
You already know about stomata in leaf where
gaseous exchange takes place in plants.
There are
other areas on the plant body as well through which
gaseous exchange take place like surface of aerial
roots, lenticels on stem etc.
Some plants have
specialized structures like breathing roots of
mangrove plants that produces oxygen is also
required by plants to produce energy and carbon
dioxide is released.
2.9.1 Transportation of gases in plants
The stomatal openings lead to a series of spaces
between the cells inside the plant.
Which form a
continuous network all over the plant.
The spaces
are very large in the leaves, much smaller in other
parts of the plant.
The air spaces are lined with water
where the oxygen is dissolved in this and passes
through the porous cell walls into the cytoplasm.
Here the glucose is broken down into carbon dioxide
and water with the liberation of the energy.
The
energy released is stored in mitochondria in the form
of A TP to perform metabolic activities.
The carbon dioxide passes out into the air spaces
by a similar method.
The whole system works by
diffusion as the oxygen is used up by the cells a
gradient develops between the cells and the air in
the spaces.

What are fossils?
Fossils are evidences of ancient life forms or ancient habitats
which have been preserved by natural processes.
Fossil evidence
is typically preserved within the sediments deposited beneath
water and land.
They can be actual remains of once lived such as bones or
seeds or even traces of past event such as dinosaur foot print or
ripple marks on a pre-historic shore.
Usually when organisms
die, their bodies will be decomposed and lost.
Sometimes the body or some parts of
the body do not decompose completely.
For example if a dead insect get caught in mud,
it will not decompose quickly and the mud will eventually harden and retain the

9.4.1 Story of Kolleru Lake
Fresh water lakes provide the nutritional requirements of the world’s
Fig-8: Kolleru Lake
poorest people.
One such lake is Kolleru which is not an ordinary wetland.
It is one of the largest fresh water lakes in India, existing between West
Godavari and Krishna districts of the state of Andhra Pradesh.
The
catchment of the lake extends up to 6121 km2.
The lake Kolleru discharges
its excess water in to the Bay of Bengal through the twisty channel called
Upputeru, which is about 60 km long.
Nevertheless, the Kolleru wetland receives
huge quantity of nutrient rich sediments from
the flood plains of these rivers.
In November 1999, the Government of
India had declared the lake as Bird Sanctuary.
214 Our Environment
This lake is hosting 193 species of birds and a variety of flora and fauna,
including medicinal plants.
It attracts migratory birds from northern Asia
and Eastern Europe between the months of October and March and it is
estimated as 20,00,000 birds per year.
The lake was also an important
habitat for an estimated 20 million residents.
This largest fresh water lake
has not only shrunk in size but faced great threat due to pollution in the
last three decades as revealed by satellite pictures.
The decrease in water
area and muddy ground in the lake resulted in flooding problems in the
lake area.

Being a profitable business, Aquaculture in Kolleru was started
extensively in the eighties which later spread to other areas in the Krishna
Godavari delta and attracted a large number of investors to the area.
In
1996, almost entire lake was brought under cultivation and bunds were
constructed to keep water out to protect the crops.
This diversion affected
the natural flow system of the lake.
The water holding capacity of the lake
is also found significantly reduced.
In due course of time activities such as agriculture and industries
came along in ever growing intensity in the catchment area of the lake.
Consequently, the drains and rivulets carry substantial quantity of various
types of pollutants into the lake.

What are fossils?
Fossils are evidences of ancient life forms or ancient habitats
which have been preserved by natural processes.
Fossil evidence
is typically preserved within the sediments deposited beneath
water and land.
They can be actual remains of once lived such as bones or
seeds or even traces of past event such as dinosaur foot print or
ripple marks on a pre-historic shore.
Usually when organisms
die, their bodies will be decomposed and lost.
Sometimes the body or some parts of
the body do not decompose completely.

it will not decompose quickly and the mud will eventually harden and retain the

12 GEN-BIO-012

Write the differences between mitosis and meiosis?

Required answer points

  • Mitosis has one division; meiosis has two
  • Mitosis forms two daughter cells; meiosis forms four
  • Mitosis preserves chromosome number; meiosis halves it
  • Mitosis supports growth/repair; meiosis forms gametes
  • Meiosis creates variation through recombination/segregation

Optional answer points

  • Compare prophase events and homologous chromosomes

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • Meiosis produces genetically identical diploid cells

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

Mitosis and meiosis are both processes of cell division, but they have several key differences. Mitosis is the process by which a single cell divides into two identical daughter cells. It occurs in somatic (body) cells and is responsible for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction. Meiosis, on the other hand, is a specialized form of cell division that occurs in the reproductive organs to produce gametes (sperm and eggs) for sexual reproduction. Meiosis results in four daughter cells, each with half the number of chromosomes as the parent cell. Mitosis involves one division, while meiosis involves two successive divisions. Additionally, meiosis includes a process called crossing over, where genetic material is exchanged between homologous chromosomes, increasing genetic diversity. In contrast, mitosis does not involve crossing over. Mitosis ensures genetic continuity, while meiosis ensures genetic variation.

Cells in some organs, such as heart and brain of an individual may
divide slowly. On the other hand bone marrow cells may actively divide to
produce red blood cells, which have a short life span nearly 120 days in
the body. For example, if you cut your finger and bleed, soon a blood clot
forms to stop the bleeding. This brings in various chemicals to the site
that stimulate skin cells to divide and heal the wound. Cell division ceases
as the wound is completely healed. In contrast, cancer cells do not respond
to such growth regulating factors and continuously divide at the expense
of normal cells, thus ultimately killing the host. So it becomes important
to understand the processes involved in cell division. The cell cycle will
help us understand this better.
6.14 Cell cycle
The process of cell division is a
very small part of the cell cycle. It
completes in 40-60 minutes. The
period between two cell divisions is
called ‘Interphase’. This is actually the
period when the genetic material
(DNA) makes its copy so that it is
equally distributed to the daughter cells
during mitosis. Interphase can be
divided into three phases.
1) G1 phase: This is the linking
period between the completion of
mitosis and the beginning of DNA replication (Gap 1 phase). The
cell size increases during this period.
2) S phase: This is the period of DNA synthesis (Synthesis phase)
leading duplication of chromosomes.
3) G2 phase: This is the time between the end of DNA replication and
the beginning of mitosis.(Gap 2 phase). Cell organelles divide and
prepare chromosome for mitosis.

M phase: This is cell division phase. It includes prophase, metaphase,

To understand the functional relationship between these phases, Potu
Narasimha Rao and Johnson (see annexure) conducted some experiments
using the cell fusion technique. That is combining two cells in experimental
conditions. With this cell fusion technique they revealed for the first time
the structure of interphase (G1, S and G2) chromosomes that are not
ordinarily visible under the microscope. They provided evidence on
progression of cells through the cell cycle in sequential unidirectional
and controlled way by a series of chemical signals that can diffuse freely
between nucleus and cytoplasm. These experiments are considered to be
a ‘mile stone’ in the cell cycle studies.

Table-1: Mitosis
6.14.1 Meiosis
Unlike mitosis which is a continuous process for division in most of
the cells. Meiosis occurs only during the formation of gametes in sexual
reproduction. Meiosis has two phases. During the first phase of meiosis
the parent cell containing two sets of chromosomes (diploid) divides and
daughter cells containg one set of chromosomes (haploid) are formed.
The second phase of meiosis is similar to normal mitosis. Thus the four
daughter cells have just half the number of chromosomes of the parent cell.
Stage Description
1. Prophase 1. Chromosomes condense and get coiled. They become visible even in
light microscope and nucleoli become smaller.
2. Chromosomes split lengthwise to form chromatids, connected by
centromeres.
3. Nuclear membrane disappears.
4. Centrosome, containing rod-like centrioles, divide and form ends
of spindle (probably animal cells only).
(Note: No pairing of chromosomes as in meiosis).
2. Metaphase 1. Chromosomes move to cell equator, spindle fibres attached to
centromeres.
3. Anaphase 1. Centromeres split, separating the chromatids.
2. Spindle fibres attached to centromeres contract, pulling chromatids
towards poles
4. Telophase 1. Chromatids elongate, become invisible, replication at this stage to
become chromosomes.
2. Nuclear membranes form round daughter nuclei.
3. Necleolus is resynthesized in each daughter nucleus.
Cytokinesis 1. Nucleus divides into two and division of cytoplasm starts Two cells
are formed.
2. Cell membrane pinches to form daughter cells (animals) or new cell
wall material becomes laid down across spindle equator (plants)

takes place while general body growth is still going on. Therefore,
some degree of sexual maturation does not necessarily mean that the body
or the mind is ready for sexual acts. Further, it is not fit for having and
bringing up children. How do we decide if the body or the mind is ready
for this major responsibility? All of us are under many different kinds of
pressures about these issues. There can be pressure from our friends for

GPT-4o API — Gold evidence

gold

Mitosis and meiosis are two different types of cell division processes. Here are the differences between them: 1. **Purpose**: - **Mitosis**: It is involved in the growth and repair of tissues. It helps in producing two identical daughter cells from a single parent cell, maintaining the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell. - **Meiosis**: It occurs during the formation of gametes in sexual reproduction. It reduces the chromosome number by half, resulting in four haploid daughter cells. 2. **Number of Divisions**: - **Mitosis**: Involves one division cycle, resulting in two daughter cells. - **Meiosis**: Involves two division cycles (Meiosis I and Meiosis II), resulting in four daughter cells. 3. **Chromosome Number**: - **Mitosis**: The daughter cells have the same diploid number of chromosomes as the parent cell. - **Meiosis**: The daughter cells have half the haploid number of chromosomes compared to the parent cell. 4. **Genetic Variation**: - **Mitosis**: Produces genetically identical cells, with no variation. - **Meiosis**: Increases genetic variation through processes like crossing over and independent assortment. 5. **Occurrence**: - **Mitosis**: Occurs in somatic (body) cells. - **Meiosis**: Occurs in germ cells during the formation of gametes. These differences are crucial for understanding how organisms grow, repair tissues, and reproduce.

Local Qwen — Retrieved evidence

Mitosis and meiosis are two types of cell division, but they have several key differences. Mitosis occurs in all body cells and results in two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell. It retains the same number of chromosomes (2n). Meiosis, on the other hand, occurs only in sex cells (gametes) and results in four daughter cells that have half the number of chromosomes (n). This is called reduction division. Mitosis is a single process, while meiosis consists of two phases. Additionally, meiosis involves the pairing and exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes, which does not occur in mitosis. These differences are important for understanding how organisms grow, repair, and reproduce.

Cells in some organs, such as heart and brain of an individual may
divide slowly.
On the other hand bone marrow cells may actively divide to
produce red blood cells, which have a short life span nearly 120 days in
the body.
For example, if you cut your finger and bleed, soon a blood clot
forms to stop the bleeding.
This brings in various chemicals to the site
that stimulate skin cells to divide and heal the wound.
Cell division ceases
as the wound is completely healed.
In contrast, cancer cells do not respond
to such growth regulating factors and continuously divide at the expense
of normal cells, thus ultimately killing the host.
So it becomes important
to understand the processes involved in cell division.
The cell cycle will
help us understand this better.

Mitosis and meiosis are two types of cell division processes that serve different purposes in living organisms. 1. **Purpose**: - **Mitosis**: This process occurs in all body cells and is responsible for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction. It ensures that each daughter cell receives an identical set of chromosomes as the parent cell. - **Meiosis**: This process occurs only in sex cells (gametes) and is crucial for sexual reproduction. It reduces the chromosome number by half, resulting in haploid cells, which is essential for maintaining the species' chromosome number through generations. 2. **Chromosome Number**: - **Mitosis**: The chromosome number remains the same as the parent cell. If the parent cell is diploid (2n), the daughter cells will also be diploid. - **Meiosis**: The chromosome number is halved. A diploid parent cell (2n) produces haploid (n) daughter cells. 3. **Number of Divisions**: - **Mitosis**: Involves one division cycle, resulting in two daughter cells. - **Meiosis**: Involves two division cycles (meiosis I and meiosis II), resulting in four daughter cells. 4. **Genetic Variation**: - **Mitosis**: Produces genetically identical cells, with no variation from the parent cell. - **Meiosis**: Increases genetic variation through processes like crossing over and independent assortment, which shuffle genetic material. 5. **Occurrence**: - **Mitosis**: Occurs in somatic (body) cells. - **Meiosis**: Occurs in germ cells during the formation of gametes (sperm and eggs). These differences highlight the distinct roles that mitosis and meiosis play in the life cycle of organisms, with mitosis focusing on growth and maintenance, and meiosis ensuring genetic diversity and proper chromosome number in offspring.

During the first phase of meiosis
the parent cell containing two sets of chromosomes (diploid) divides and
daughter cells containg one set of chromosomes (haploid) are formed.
The second phase of meiosis is similar to normal mitosis.
Thus the four
daughter cells have just half the number of chromosomes of the parent cell.
Stage Description
1.
Prophase 1.
Chromosomes condense and get coiled.
They become visible even in
light microscope and nucleoli become smaller.
2.
Chromosomes split lengthwise to form chromatids, connected by
centromeres.
3.
Nuclear membrane disappears.
4.
Centrosome, containing rod-like centrioles, divide and form ends
of spindle (probably animal cells only).
(Note: No pairing of chromosomes as in meiosis).
2.
Metaphase 1.
Chromosomes move to cell equator, spindle fibres attached to
centromeres.
3.
Anaphase 1.
Centromeres split, separating the chromatids.
2.
Spindle fibres attached to centromeres contract, pulling chromatids
towards poles
4.
Telophase 1.
Chromatids elongate, become invisible, replication at this stage to
become chromosomes.
2.
Nuclear membranes form round daughter nuclei.
3.
Necleolus is resynthesized in each daughter nucleus.
Cytokinesis 1.
Nucleus divides into two and division of cytoplasm starts Two cells
are formed.
2.
Cell membrane pinches to form daughter cells (animals) or new cell
wall material becomes laid down across spindle equator (plants)
Reflection of light at curved surfacesReproduction145
Hence meiosis is also called as Reduction Division.
The daughter
cells are haploid in condition.
You will learn more about this in further
classes.

As we have seen, the process of sexual maturation is gradual, and
takes place while general body growth is still going on.
Therefore,
some degree of sexual maturation does not necessarily mean that the body
or the mind is ready for sexual acts.
Further, it is not fit for having and
bringing up children.
How do we decide if the body or the mind is ready
for this major responsibility?
All of us are under many different kinds of
pressures about these issues.
There can be pressure from our friends for
participating in many activities, whether we really want or not.
There
can be pressure from families to get married and start having children.

There can be pressure from government and voluntary organisations to

In the lesson 8th class “why do we fall ill”, we learnt that the diseases
can be transmitted from person to person in a variety of ways.
Since the
sexual act is a very intimate connection of bodies, it is not surprising
that many diseases can be sexually transmitted.
These include bacterial
infections such as Gonorrhea and syphilis, and viral infections such as
AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome).
These diseases spread by unsafe sexual contacts, using infected
devices, infected blood transfusion, from an infected mother to child.
Unfortunetely, Telangana state has high incidents of HIV positive
cases.
Illiteracy, poor health, unemployment, migration, non-traditional
sex practise, unethical contacts and trafficking are some of the factors
contributing to the spread of HIV in the state, according to experts.
The government established Anti Retroviral Therapy (ART
centres) to supply medicine to HIV patients.
Medical and health,
family health departments AIDS control projects implementing
various programmes like ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist),
Red Ribbon Express, etc., to create awareness in society on the risks
and symptoms of AIDS.

176 Heredity and Evolution
When we observe our world and its myriad forms of life, we are struck
by two seemingly opposite observations, the fantastic variety of life and
the similarity between them.
As we shall see, we would need to understand
these two characteristics of life in order to comprehend how life evolves.
When we say that something evolves, we mean not only that it changes,
but that there is also some component of direction in that change.
But, how does evolution take place?
Does it occur in a slow and steady
manner or in quick jumps?
Is it just about change and producing something
new and different?
In the chapter on reproduction we have studied that reproductive
processes usually give rise to individuals that have some new characters
in spite of the similarity that they share with their parents.
Often such new
characters give rise to observable changes in life forms.
x How are new characters produced?
x Are they inherited?
x Do they have any role in the process of evolution?
In this chapter we shall discuss all of the above.

8.2 Mendel and his experiments
Over centuries variations and their role in nature have been studied by
naturalists.
During early 19th century, a lot of work was done by several
scientists.
Some of these studies will help us to understand how variations
occur and are transferred from one generation to the next.
We shall study
a detailed account of experimental evidences provided by Gregor Johann
Mendel in the early 19th century who is known as ‘Father of genetics’.
Reflection of light at curved surfaces179 Heredity and Evolution
In 1857 Gregor Johann Mendel started working on the problem of
how variations were passed from one generation to the other.
Mendel
did not do his experimental work either in a University or in a
Laboratory.
As he was an Austrian monk in a monastery he simply did
Fig-2: Gregor
Johann Mendel
his experiments in the monastery garden.
He worked for over seven
years after which he presented the conclusions from his experimental
data in the form of a detailed research paper.
8.2.1 Reasons for selecting Pea plant
Mendel made many careful observations of plants and found that
pea plants would be most suitable to carry on further experimentation
because it has the following advantages:
1.
Well defined characters 2.
Bisexual flowers
3.
Predominently self pollinating
4.
Suitable for cross pollination
5.
It is an annual plant
Then he planned and designed experiments to find out the answers to
questions that came to his mind.
He had worked on nearly 10,000 pea
plants of 34 different varieties.
Observing pea plants carefully, Mendel noted that they differ from
one another in many ways.

How does mucus help in passage of food?

Required answer points

  • Oesophageal walls secrete mucus
  • Mucus lubricates and protects the wall
  • The bolus slides down more easily during peristalsis

Optional answer points

Prohibited / unsupported claims

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

Mucus helps in the passage of food through the oesophagus by lubricating the walls of the oesophagus. This lubrication makes it easier for the food bolus to slide down smoothly. The mucus also protects the oesophageal walls from damage, ensuring that the passage of food is efficient and safe. Additionally, the saliva in the bolus also aids in the easy movement of food into the stomach.

x Why do we salivate when you sleep during the day?
You have heard about Nocturnal animals, which are active during nights, but we
are active during daytime and take rest at night. All the systems of our body are active
in function during the time of our activity. Hence, man is a diurnal animal. Our
digestive system is also active in day time and ready to receive the food for digestion.
If we sleep during daytime saliva oozes out of our mouth and wets the pillows. This
will not happen during night time. We secrete 1-1.5 liters of saliva per day.

The walls of the food pipe secrete a slippery

The wall of the oesophagus is made up of two kinds of smooth muscles.
The inner layer consists of circular muscles and the outer layer of
longitudinal muscles. Contraction of the circular muscles results in
narrowing of the oesophagus just behind the bolus. So the food is squeezed
downwards.
Contraction of the longitudinal muscles infront of the bolus widen
the tube, this results in shortening of that particular part of the oesophagus.
Contraction and relaxation of these muscles bring in a wave like motion
that propels the food bolus into the stomach by the action called as
“peristalsis” (you have studied about this in the chapter on nutrition). This
is involuntary and under the control of autonomous nervous system.

properly or do not eat in hurry.

GPT-4o API — Gold evidence

gold

Mucus plays a crucial role in the passage of food through the oesophagus. It is a slippery substance secreted by the walls of the oesophagus, which helps to lubricate and protect the oesophageal walls from damage. This lubrication allows the food bolus to slide down easily through the oesophagus, similar to how oiled potatoes move through a tube. Additionally, the saliva present in the bolus also aids in the smooth movement of food into the stomach. This process is facilitated by the wave-like movements of the oesophagus walls, known as peristalsis, which is an involuntary action controlled by the autonomous nervous system.

We eat various types of food which pass through the same digestive
tract.
It is to be converted to substances small enough to be utilised
by our body.
This needs various processess that can be studied as
follows.
1.5.1 Passage of food through alimentary canal or gut
Food is cut and crushed by our teeth in the
mouth and mixed with saliva to make it wet and
slippery lump called bolus (This process is called
as mastication).
This bolus is suitable to pass
through oesophagus.
Saliva is secreted by three pairs
of salivary glands.
Saliva mainly contains an enzyme
amylase (ptyalin) which help in the breakdown of
complex carbohydrates into simple ones.
This
process of breaking down larger complex substances
into simple ones with the help of enzymes is called digestion.
The
tongue helps in mixing the food and pushing it into the next part.
The
lower jaw also helps in this process.
Fig-12: Location of some
salivary glands
palate
salivary duct
salivary
glands
epiglottis
tongue
uvula
We can find out the effect of salivary amylase on carbohydrates in
mouth.
To know the chemical nature of the saliva perform the activity-
7 of co-ordination in life process of this text book.
The soft food mixed with saliva passes through oesophagus or food
pipe by wave like movements called peristaltic movement to the stomach.
In the stomach, food gets churned with gastric juice and HCl rendering the
medium acidic.
Now the food is in semisolid condition.
The digestion of
food goes on as most of the proteins are broken down into smaller
molecules with the help of enzyme pepsin.
Nutrition 16
Food in the form of a soft slimy substance where some proteins and
carbohydrates have already been broken down is called chyme.
Now the
food material passes from the stomach to the small intestine.
Here the
ring like muscles called pyloric sphincters relax to open the passage into
the small intestine.
The sphincters are responsible for regulating the
opening of the passage such that only small quantities of the food material
may be passed into the small intestine at a time.
The small intestine is the longest part of the
alimentary canal.
Its proximal part is called duodenum.
It is the site of further digestion of carbohydrates,
proteins and fats.
It receives the secretion of liver and
pancreas for this purpose.
These juices render the internal
condition of the intestine gradually to a basic or alkaline one.
Fats are digested by converting them into small globule
like forms by the help of the bile juice secreted from liver.
This process is called emulsification.
Pancreatic juice secreted from pancreas contains enzymes like trypsin
for carrying on the process of digestion of proteins and lipase for fats.
Walls of the small intestine secrete intestinal juice (Succusentericus)
which carry this process further that is small molecules of proteins are
broken down to further smaller molecules.
The same is the condition with
fats.
Carbohydrate digestion that started in the mouth and did not occur in
the stomach, resumes now as the medium gradually changes to an alkaline
one and the enzymes become active for complete carbohydrate breakdown.

The wall of the oesophagus is made up of two kinds of smooth muscles.
The inner layer consists of circular muscles and the outer layer of
longitudinal muscles.
Contraction of the circular muscles results in
narrowing of the oesophagus just behind the bolus.
So the food is squeezed
downwards.
Contraction of the longitudinal muscles infront of the bolus widen
the tube, this results in shortening of that particular part of the oesophagus.
Contraction and relaxation of these muscles bring in a wave like motion
that propels the food bolus into the stomach by the action called as
“peristalsis” (you have studied about this in the chapter on nutrition).
This
is involuntary and under the control of autonomous nervous system.

Mucus plays an important role in the passage of food through the oesophagus. It is a slippery substance secreted by the walls of the oesophagus, which helps in lubricating and protecting the oesophageal walls from damage. This lubrication allows the food bolus to slide down easily through the oesophagus, similar to how oiled potatoes move through a tube. This process is aided by peristaltic movements, which are wave-like contractions and relaxations of the oesophageal muscles that propel the food towards the stomach.
