We eat various types of food which pass through the same digestive
tract.
It is to be converted to substances small enough to be utilised
by our body.
This needs various processess that can be studied as
follows.
1.5.1 Passage of food through alimentary canal or gut
Food is cut and crushed by our teeth in the
mouth and mixed with saliva to make it wet and
slippery lump called bolus (This process is called
as mastication).
This bolus is suitable to pass
through oesophagus.
Saliva is secreted by three pairs
of salivary glands.
Saliva mainly contains an enzyme
amylase (ptyalin) which help in the breakdown of
complex carbohydrates into simple ones.
This
process of breaking down larger complex substances
into simple ones with the help of enzymes is called digestion.
The
tongue helps in mixing the food and pushing it into the next part.
The
lower jaw also helps in this process.
Fig-12: Location of some
salivary glands
palate
salivary duct
salivary
glands
epiglottis
tongue
uvula
We can find out the effect of salivary amylase on carbohydrates in
mouth.
To know the chemical nature of the saliva perform the activity-
7 of co-ordination in life process of this text book.
The soft food mixed with saliva passes through oesophagus or food
pipe by wave like movements called peristaltic movement to the stomach.
In the stomach, food gets churned with gastric juice and HCl rendering the
medium acidic.
Now the food is in semisolid condition.
The digestion of
food goes on as most of the proteins are broken down into smaller
molecules with the help of enzyme pepsin.
Nutrition 16
Food in the form of a soft slimy substance where some proteins and
carbohydrates have already been broken down is called chyme.
Now the
food material passes from the stomach to the small intestine.
Here the
ring like muscles called pyloric sphincters relax to open the passage into
the small intestine.
The sphincters are responsible for regulating the
opening of the passage such that only small quantities of the food material
may be passed into the small intestine at a time.
The small intestine is the longest part of the
alimentary canal.
Its proximal part is called duodenum.
It is the site of further digestion of carbohydrates,
proteins and fats.
It receives the secretion of liver and
pancreas for this purpose.
These juices render the internal
condition of the intestine gradually to a basic or alkaline one.
Fats are digested by converting them into small globule
like forms by the help of the bile juice secreted from liver.
This process is called emulsification.
Pancreatic juice secreted from pancreas contains enzymes like trypsin
for carrying on the process of digestion of proteins and lipase for fats.
Walls of the small intestine secrete intestinal juice (Succusentericus)
which carry this process further that is small molecules of proteins are
broken down to further smaller molecules.
The same is the condition with
fats.
Carbohydrate digestion that started in the mouth and did not occur in
the stomach, resumes now as the medium gradually changes to an alkaline
one and the enzymes become active for complete carbohydrate breakdown.

14 GEN-BIO-014

Describe the acid-and-leaf experiment used to model how the stomach is protected from its own acid, and compare the observations with the stomach’s mucus lining.

Required answer points

  • Use two similar green leaves
  • Coat one with petroleum jelly/grease and leave one uncoated
  • Add equal drops of weak acid and observe
  • The uncoated leaf is affected while the coated leaf is protected
  • Petroleum jelly models the protective mucus lining of the stomach

Optional answer points

  • Observe after about half an hour

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • Mucus neutralises all stomach acid completely

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

The acid-and-leaf experiment is designed to demonstrate how the stomach is protected from its own acid. In this experiment, two similar green leaves are taken. One leaf is coated with petroleum jelly or grease, while the other is left untreated. A weak acid is then applied to both leaves. After some time, it is observed that the leaf without petroleum jelly is affected by the acid, while the leaf coated with petroleum jelly remains unaffected. This is because the petroleum jelly acts like the mucus lining in the stomach, which protects the stomach walls from the corrosive effects of stomach acid. The mucus secreted by cells in the stomach walls forms a thin lining that counteracts the acid, similar to how petroleum jelly protects the leaf from the acid.

Digestive juices are produced depending on the quantity of food
material. If the stomach would produce same amount of digestive juices
irrespective of the food quantity the walls of stomach would be destroyed.
( See annexure )
We also know that stomach secretes strong acids during digestion.
The HCl secreted by the walls of the stomach is strong enough to digest
the hard bones as well. Then how is the stomach protected from the
secretions of its own acids. To understand this we will perform the
following experiment.
Acid and leaf experiment
Take two similar green leaves from your school garden. Apply vaseline
or petroleum jelly or grease on one leaf leave the other free. Add 1 or 2
drops of some weak acid on both the leaves. Observe them after half an
hour or so and write your observation in your note book.
x What kind of change did you observe in the leaves?
x Which leaf was affected by the acid?
x What saved the other leaf from the effect of acid?
Mucus secreted by some cells present in the walls of the stomach
form a thin lining on the walls of the stomach. This counters the action of
acid. The function of petroleum jelly can be compared to that of mucus
lining the stomach walls. Hence the stomach is protected from damage
being caused by the secretion of its own acids.
7.1.8 Travel of food from the stomach to the intestine
Now food is a soup like mixture when it leaves the stomach and enters
the small intestine. When the food enters the intestine the acidic nature of
the chyme initiates the production of hormones like secretin and
cholecystokinin which stimulate pancreas, liver and walls of small intestine
to secrete pancreatic juice, bile juice and succus entericus.
x Why small intestine is like a long coiled structure?
x How the absorbtion takes place in the small intestine?
The absorption of nutrients by villi in the small intestine is a very
selective process.

The acid-and-leaf experiment is designed to model how the stomach is protected from its own acid. In this experiment, two similar green leaves are used. One leaf is coated with vaseline or petroleum jelly, while the other is left untreated. A few drops of a weak acid are added to both leaves. After some time, observations are made to see the effects of the acid on the leaves. The leaf without the protective coating is affected by the acid, showing signs of damage. In contrast, the leaf with the vaseline remains unaffected. This demonstrates how the vaseline acts as a protective barrier against the acid. This experiment is analogous to how the stomach protects itself. The stomach secretes strong acids for digestion, but it is protected by a mucus lining. This mucus acts like the vaseline, forming a barrier that prevents the acid from damaging the stomach walls. Thus, the mucus lining is crucial in protecting the stomach from its own acidic secretions.

The digestive tract is unique among internal
organs because it is exposed to a large variety of
physiochemical stimuli from the external world in
the form of ingested food.
As a consequence, the
intestine has developed a rich store of co ordinated
movements of its muscular apparatus along with
neural apparatus to ensure the appropriate mixing and
propulsion of contents during digestion, absorption,
and excretion.Fig-9: Schematic

168 Coordination in life processes
The neural apparatus of our digestive tract comprises of such a vast
and complicated network of neurons that it has been nicknamed by scientists
as the second brain!
Research in this area is currently investigating how
the second brain mediates the body’s immune response; after all, at least
70 percent of our immune system is aimed at the gut to expel and kill
foreign invaders.
Scientists are also working to find out how trillions of bacteria in the
gut communicate with the cells of gut nervous system.
A deeper
understanding of this mass of neural tissue, filled with important
'neurotransmitters', is revealing that it does much more than merely handle
digestion or inflict the occasional nervous pang of hunger.
The little brain
in our inner yards, in connection with the big one in our skull, partly
determines our mental state and plays key roles in certain diseases

Martin alive the next day as he never expected so.

For centuries stomach was thought to cook food by producing heat.
Also theStomach
was viewed as a mill,a fermenting vat or a stew pan.
Through his experiments Dr.Beaumonts
experiments revolutioned the concepts of digestion.
June -on16,1822 became the beginning
for the the most pioneering experiments in medicine.
He recounted many of his
observations and experiments in his journal which says “I consider myself but a humble
experimentor “ in which the information provided still obeyed scientific method basing all
the inferences on direct experimentation.
Some of the discoveries of Dr.Beaumont were.

there was no change or alteration in temperature.
He found the temperature being
maintained constant ( 1000F/380C ).

previous opinions that gastric was nothing but contains simply water.

some authors as the most general solvent in nature and of the alimentary canal.
Even
the hardest bone cannot with stand its action .Even outside the stomach its capable of
effecting digestion.
Based on the evidences he concluded that HCl as chemical agent
that aids in chemical reaction.
3) He found Gastric juice is not stored in the stomach.
But ,is secreted when the food is
taken.
When the food enters the stomach it excites the vessels to discharge its contents
immediately for digestion.
4) He understood that digestion begins immediately when the food enters the stomach.
He tested the contents of the stomach exactly 20min. after taking food (dinner containing
ordinary food of boiled and salted beef, potatoes ,bread, beef and turnips) by collecting
the fluids from the flap and found digestion had commenced and was progressing well
at that time.

(food reaching the stomach without passing the mouth and oesophagus).

his assumptions he made St.
Martin fast from breakfast time till 4’0 Clock and then
introduced food into the stomach through the flap.
The sensation of hunger subsided.

The neural apparatus of our digestive tract comprises of such a vast
and complicated network of neurons that it has been nicknamed by scientists
as the second brain!
Research in this area is currently investigating how
the second brain mediates the body’s immune response; after all, at least
70 percent of our immune system is aimed at the gut to expel and kill
foreign invaders.
Scientists are also working to find out how trillions of bacteria in the
gut communicate with the cells of gut nervous system.
A deeper
understanding of this mass of neural tissue, filled with important
'neurotransmitters', is revealing that it does much more than merely handle
digestion or inflict the occasional nervous pang of hunger.
The little brain
in our inner yards, in connection with the big one in our skull, partly
determines our mental state and plays key roles in certain diseases

Explain Mendel’s monohybrid experiment with an example. Which law of inheritance does it demonstrate?

Required answer points

  • Cross pure parents differing in one trait
  • F₁ shows only the dominant trait
  • Self the F₁ heterozygotes
  • F₂ phenotype ratio is about 3:1 and genotype ratio 1:2:1
  • Relate results to dominance and segregation

Optional answer points

  • Use Y/y or another textbook trait and a checkerboard

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • Recessive factors disappear permanently in F₁

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

Mendel’s monohybrid experiment involved crossing pea plants with different traits to study how these traits are inherited. He selected pea plants that produced either yellow or green seeds. The yellow seed plants were pure (YY) and the green seed plants were also pure (yy). When these plants were cross-pollinated, all the offspring in the first generation (F1) had yellow seeds. This is because the yellow trait is dominant over the green trait. When these F1 plants were self-pollinated, the second generation (F2) showed a 3:1 ratio of yellow to green seeds. This ratio indicates that the green trait, which was hidden in the F1 generation, reappeared in the F2 generation. This experiment demonstrates Mendel’s Law of Dominance, which states that in a pair of alleles, the dominant trait is expressed in the first generation, while the recessive trait remains hidden but can reappear in the second generation.

8.2.3 Monohybrid Cross
A cross-pollination between a pure breed of yellow seed
bearing plant and green seed bearing plant gave the following
results :
First Filial / F1-generation : (Filial means progeny)
All pea seeds were Yellow. On self-pollination of these pea
plants the following results were obtained :
All pea seeds were yellow
Second Filial / F2-generation : The F2 generation had about
75% of yellow seeded pea plants and 25% of green seeded
pea plants, i.e. they appear in 3 : 1 ratio.
Adding to above results, Mendel made following
obseravtions :
1. A set of peas (about 25%) obtained in F2 generation are
yellow seeded plants (Homozygous dominant).
2. A Set of peas (about 50%) obtained in F2 generation are
heterozygous yellow and give yellow and green seeds in
3:1 on self pollination.
3. A set of peas (about 25%) obtained in F2 generation are
green seeded. On self-pollination they keep producing
green seeded plants (Homozygous recessive).

Mendel made some assumptions by which he could explain his
observations.
Assumption 1: Every pea plant has two ‘factors’ which are responsible
for producing a particular character or trait. The determining agent
responsible for each trait is called a factor.
Mendel carefully choose the plants which did not produce a mixed
result (pure). In our example of yellow and green peas, a pure breed
(parental stage) will have both the ‘factors’ of the same type.
A pure breed (parental) yellow seed producing pea will have both the
‘factors’ of the same type. Let us denote them by ‘YY’.

A pure breed (parental) green seed producing pea will also have both
the ‘factors’ of the same type. Let us denote them by ‘yy’.
YY and yy are called homozygous as the factors in them are same. If
the combination is Yy then it is called heterozygous.
Assumption-2 : During reproduction one ‘factor’ from each parent is
taken to form a new pair in the progeny.
Assumption-3 : One of these will always dominate the other if mixed
together. The trait expressed in F1 generation is called dominant. While
the other which did not express in F1 is called recessive.Assume that ‘Y’
(the one causing yellow colour) is a dominating ‘factor’. That means if ‘Y’
and ‘y’ come together ‘Y’ will dominate. Then the pea seeds will be always

8.2.5 F2-Generation
So in this heap we will get approximately equal number of YY, Yy, yY
and yy peas. But any pea that has a Y factor will be yellow. Any pea that has
both yy will be green. Since all combinations are equally likely:
1. YY will be approximately 25% and is yellow.
2. yY will be approximately 25% and is yellow, Yy will be approximately
25 % and is yellow
3. yy will be approximately 25% and is green.
Some seeds appear yellow in colour in F1 generation. When these
seeds were sown some of the plants produced green coloured seeds. So
we can’t determine internal character based on external visible character.
8.2.6 Phenotype
Thus in F2 generation we can clearly observe that 75 percent are yellow
seed producing pea plants and 25 percent are green ones. This is known as
‘Phenotype’(externally visible characters) and this ratio is called
‘phenotypic ratio’ or monohybrid phenotype ratio. It is 3:1.
8.2.7 Genotype
Genetically, in 75 percent yellow seed producing pea plants only 25
percent pea plants produce yellow seeds that are pure breeds (YY) and are
‘homozygous’ that is to have the same factors for representing a character.
Remaining 50 percent yellow seed producing pea plants are (Yy)
heterozygous . The remaining 25 percent green seed producing pea plants
are pure (yy) homozygous type.
The constitution of pea plants as shown by the representative letters Y
and y to show the probable nature of factors is known as genotype. This
ratio is known as genotypic ratio or monohybrid genotype ratio. It is
1:2:1. (25:50:25)

8.2.9 Mendel’s Laws
Mendel propounded that, among a pair of closely related ‘alleles’ or
factors for a character, only one expresses itself in the first generation as
one of the allele is dominant over the other. This is so evident that it came
to be called as Mendel’s Law of Dominance.
For expression of each character a pair of factors or alleles are
responsible. Each one of these alleles is received from each parent. When
this generation forms gametes, these alleles get separate and each one
enters into a separate gamete randomly. This separation of alleles at the
time of formation of gametes is called law of Segregation.
Mendel also explained the process of inheritance of more than one
character. For this, he proposed law of Independent Assortment. We
will learn more about this in further classes, for the basic understanding
refer in annexure.
Traits that may be passed on from one generation to the next are called
as heritable traits. We have studied some of them for the pea plant, in the
experiments conducted by Mendel.

8.2.5 F2-Generation
So in this heap we will get approximately equal number of YY, Yy, yY

25 % and is yellow
3. yy will be approximately 25% and is green.
Some seeds appear yellow in colour in F1 generation. When these
seeds were sown some of the plants produced green coloured seeds. So
we can’t determine internal character based on external visible character.
8.2.6 Phenotype
Thus in F2 generation we can clearly observe that 75 percent are yellow
seed producing pea plants and 25 percent are green ones. This is known as
‘Phenotype’(externally visible characters) and this ratio is called
‘phenotypic ratio’ or monohybrid phenotype ratio. It is 3:1.
8.2.7 Genotype
Genetically, in 75 percent yellow seed producing pea plants only 25
percent pea plants produce yellow seeds that are pure breeds (YY) and are
‘homozygous’ that is to have the same factors for representing a character.
Remaining 50 percent yellow seed producing pea plants are (Yy)
heterozygous . The remaining 25 percent green seed producing pea plants
are pure (yy) homozygous type.
The constitution of pea plants as shown by the representative letters Y
and y to show the probable nature of factors is known as genotype. This
ratio is known as genotypic ratio or monohybrid genotype ratio. It is
1:2:1. (25:50:25)

8.2.9 Mendel’s Laws
Mendel propounded that, among a pair of closely related ‘alleles’ or
factors for a character, only one expresses itself in the first generation as
one of the allele is dominant over the other. This is so evident that it came
to be called as Mendel’s Law of Dominance.
For expression of each character a pair of factors or alleles are
responsible. Each one of these alleles is received from each parent. When
this generation forms gametes, these alleles get separate and each one
enters into a separate gamete randomly. This separation of alleles at the
time of formation of gametes is called law of Segregation.
Mendel also explained the process of inheritance of more than one
character. For this, he proposed law of Independent Assortment. We
will learn more about this in further classes, for the basic understanding
refer in annexure.
Traits that may be passed on from one generation to the next are called
as heritable traits. We have studied some of them for the pea plant, in the
experiments conducted by Mendel.

Local Qwen — Retrieved evidence

Mendel’s monohybrid experiment involved studying the inheritance of a single trait, such as seed color in pea plants. He selected two purebred pea plants—one with yellow seeds and one with green seeds. When he crossed these plants, all the offspring in the first generation (F1) had yellow seeds. This demonstrated that the yellow seed color was dominant over the green seed color. When these F1 plants were allowed to self-pollinate, the second generation (F2) showed a 3:1 ratio of yellow to green seeds. This ratio indicated that the recessive trait (green seeds) reappeared in the F2 generation. This experiment demonstrated Mendel’s Law of Dominance, which states that in a pair of alleles, the dominant trait is expressed in the presence of the recessive trait.

years after which he presented the conclusions from his experimental
data in the form of a detailed research paper.
8.2.1 Reasons for selecting Pea plant
Mendel made many careful observations of plants and found that
pea plants would be most suitable to carry on further experimentation
because it has the following advantages:
1.
Well defined characters 2.
Bisexual flowers
3.
Predominently self pollinating
4.
Suitable for cross pollination
5.
It is an annual plant
Then he planned and designed experiments to find out the answers to
questions that came to his mind.
He had worked on nearly 10,000 pea
plants of 34 different varieties.
Observing pea plants carefully, Mendel noted that they differ from
one another in many ways.

8.2.9 Mendel’s Laws
Mendel propounded that, among a pair of closely related ‘alleles’ or
factors for a character, only one expresses itself in the first generation as
one of the allele is dominant over the other.
This is so evident that it came
to be called as Mendel’s Law of Dominance.
For expression of each character a pair of factors or alleles are
responsible.
Each one of these alleles is received from each parent.
When
this generation forms gametes, these alleles get separate and each one
enters into a separate gamete randomly.
This separation of alleles at the
time of formation of gametes is called law of Segregation.
Mendel also explained the process of inheritance of more than one
character.
For this, he proposed law of Independent Assortment.
We
will learn more about this in further classes, for the basic understanding
refer in annexure.
Traits that may be passed on from one generation to the next are called
as heritable traits.
We have studied some of them for the pea plant, in the
experiments conducted by Mendel.

16 GEN-BIO-016

How does sex determination take place in humans?

Required answer points

  • Females are XX and males are XY
  • Ova carry only X
  • Sperm carry either X or Y
  • X-bearing sperm plus X ovum gives XX; Y-bearing sperm plus X ovum gives XY
  • The fertilising sperm determines chromosomal sex

Optional answer points

  • Expected probability is approximately equal for XX and XY

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • The mother’s ovum can carry Y

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

In humans, sex determination occurs through the combination of sex chromosomes present in the gametes (sperm and ovum) of the parents. Each human cell contains 23 pairs of chromosomes, of which 22 pairs are autosomes (non-sex chromosomes), and the remaining pair are sex chromosomes. Females have two X chromosomes (XX), while males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). All the ova (eggs) produced by a woman contain only X chromosomes. The sperm produced by a man, however, can have either an X or a Y chromosome. If a sperm carrying an X chromosome fertilizes the ovum, the resulting zygote will have XX chromosomes and develop into a female. If a sperm carrying a Y chromosome fertilizes the ovum, the resulting zygote will have XY chromosomes and develop into a male. Thus, the sex of the baby is determined by the type of sperm that fertilizes the egg.

Sex determination in human beings

GPT-4o API — Gold evidence

gold

In humans, sex determination is controlled by the sex chromosomes, which are a specific pair of chromosomes among the 23 pairs present in each cell. Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes, which are chromosomes that do not differ between males and females. The 23rd pair consists of the sex chromosomes, which are either X or Y. Females have two X chromosomes (XX), while males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). During reproduction, the mother provides an X chromosome in all her eggs, while the father can provide either an X or a Y chromosome in his sperm. If a sperm carrying an X chromosome fertilizes the egg, the resulting combination is XX, and the baby will be female. If a sperm carrying a Y chromosome fertilizes the egg, the combination is XY, and the baby will be male. Therefore, the sex of the baby is determined by the type of sperm that fertilizes the egg, making the father responsible for determining the sex of the baby.

In humans, sex determination occurs through the combination of sex chromosomes inherited from the parents. The father contributes either an X or a Y chromosome, while the mother always contributes an X chromosome. If the father's sperm carries an X chromosome, the resulting zygote will have XX chromosomes and develop into a female. If the sperm carries a Y chromosome, the zygote will have XY chromosomes and develop into a male. This process is explained in the textbook, which states that females have two X chromosomes (XX) and males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). The gametes from the father are of two types: one with an X chromosome and one with a Y chromosome. The mother's gametes (ova) always have an X chromosome. The sex of the baby is determined at the moment of fertilization when the sperm and egg combine.

Chromosomes whose number and morphology do not differ between
males and females of a species are called autosomes.
The remaining pair
is called allosomes or sex chromosomes.
These are of two types, one is
‘X’ and the other is ‘Y’.
These two chromosomes determine the sex of an
individual.
Females have two ‘X’ chromosomes in their cells (XX).
Males
have one ‘X’ and one ‘Y’ chromosomes in their cells (XY).
All the gametes
(ova) produced by a woman have only X chromosomes.
The gametes
(sperm) produced by a man are of two types one with X chromosome and
the other one with Y chromosome.
If the sperm carries Y chromosome
and fertilizes the ovum (X chromosome) then the baby will have XY
condition.
So the baby will be a boy.

In this situation a colour variation arises during reproduction.
So that

Fig-5: Red and green beetles
More over this green coloured beetle passes its colour to its off spring
(Progeny).
So that all its progeny are green.
Crows cannot see the green
coloured beetles on green leaves of the bushes and therefore crows cannot
eat them.
But crows can see the red beetles and eat them.
As a result there
are more and more green beetles than red ones which decrease in their
number.
The variation of colour in beetle ‘green’ gave a survival advantage to
‘green beetles’ than red beetles.
In other words it was naturally selected.
We can see that the ‘natural selection’ was exerted by the crows.

retrieved

In humans, sex determination is controlled by specific chromosomes known as sex chromosomes. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes, out of which 22 pairs are autosomes and the remaining pair is the sex chromosomes. These sex chromosomes are of two types: X and Y. Females have two X chromosomes (XX), while males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). During reproduction, the mother contributes an X chromosome to the offspring through her egg, as all her eggs carry an X chromosome. The father can contribute either an X or a Y chromosome through his sperm. If the sperm carrying an X chromosome fertilizes the egg, the resulting combination is XX, and the baby will be female. If the sperm carrying a Y chromosome fertilizes the egg, the combination is XY, and the baby will be male. Therefore, it is the father’s sperm that determines the sex of the baby, not the mother.

Chromosomes whose number and morphology do not differ between
males and females of a species are called autosomes.
The remaining pair
is called allosomes or sex chromosomes.
These are of two types, one is
‘X’ and the other is ‘Y’.
These two chromosomes determine the sex of an
individual.
Females have two ‘X’ chromosomes in their cells (XX).
Males
have one ‘X’ and one ‘Y’ chromosomes in their cells (XY).
All the gametes
(ova) produced by a woman have only X chromosomes.
The gametes
(sperm) produced by a man are of two types one with X chromosome and
the other one with Y chromosome.
If the sperm carries Y chromosome
and fertilizes the ovum (X chromosome) then the baby will have XY
condition.
So the baby will be a boy.

17 GEN-BIO-017

What happens to the amount of energy transferred from one step to the next in a food chain?

Required answer points

  • Available energy decreases at each trophic transfer
  • Only a small fraction becomes new biomass
  • Energy is lost through respiration, activity, heat, and undigested material
  • This limits food-chain length

Optional answer points

  • Many animals convert no more than about 10% of food into body tissue

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • Energy increases toward the top trophic level

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

In a food chain, the amount of energy transferred from one step to the next decreases. This is because only a small proportion of the energy from one trophic level is passed on to the next. For example, when animals eat, only a small part of their food is converted into new tissue, which forms the food for the next trophic level. The rest of the energy is used for the animal's life processes, such as staying alive, or is lost as heat or waste. Typically, only about 10% of the energy from one level is transferred to the next, with the majority being lost as heat or through metabolic processes.

The biomass in a trophic level may be more or less than the other
trophic levels. Biomass is a measure of the amount of food available. When
animals eat, only a small proportion of their food is converted into new
tissue, which inturn forms the food for the next trophic level. Part of
biomass that animals eat is used to provide energy needed for staying alive,
rest passes out of its body.
The biomass pyramid shows that animals are relatively inefficient in
converting food into body tissues, the remaining part of the food being
undigested is passed out as waste, or broken down in respiration to supply
energy for activities such as feeding. Many animals convert not more than
10% of their food into their body tissues, in some herbivores, it is even
less. Let us take an example of a food chain which has been worked out in
some detail- one in which we are involved when we eat fish. In this chain
the phytoplankton on the surface water of sea are food producers. They
trap energy from sunlight. The zooplankton feed on the microscopic plants
and the fish in turn feed on the zooplankton; we are at the end of the chain
when we eat the fish.
9.3.3 Pyramid of Energy
Food is the source of energy for organisms
that are used in the growth and rebuilding the
parts of the body; that are constantly wearing out.
The food by its nature is the chemical energy
and as in stored form, it is potential energy. There
are several mechanisms in organisms for
continuous absorption of materials for the
production of organic material, and for the
release and conversion of organic material into
inorganic form. Plants absorb the minerals from the soil. They are absorbed
into the plant through roots.
Photosynthesis is an essential process for the life. The energy in
sunlight, carbon dioxide and the water which are needed by all living things
belong to nonliving things. As a result of photosynthesis, these can be
made available in a suitable form of energy the food to the world of living
things the animals or consumers, only by the green plants the producers.
The food chains and food webs help in the transfer of the food and energy
from the producers to different consumers.

212 Our EnvironmentGovernment’s Gift for Students’ Progress
Animals obtain the minerals from the plant or animal food or both.
Thus the mineral matter is constantly being removed from the earth to
become a part of the plant, which may become a part of animal body.
Try to identify the basic sources of various foods we eat. For example
curd that we eat is processed from milk, which comes from a cow, which
in turn eats grass. The grass carries out photosynthesis and prepares food.
In every case, the origin of food materials can be traced back to green
plants.
Once the food is eaten, its energy follows a variety of pattern through
the organisms. Not all the food can be fully digested and assimilated. Hair,
feathers, insect exoskeletons, cartilage and bone in animal foods, cellulose
and lignin in plant foods cannot be digested by the most animals. These
materials are either ejected by defecation or regurgitated as indigested
remains.
Assimilated energy (that is not lost through respiration or excretion)
is available for the synthesis of new biomass through growth and
reproduction. Organisms lose some biomass by death, disease or annual
leaf-drop, where they enter the detritus pathways of the food chain i.e.,
after the death and decomposition of organisms the materials flow back
into the environment(soil, water, air). The remaining biomass is eventually
consumed by herbivores or predators and its energy there by enters the
next higher trophic level in the ecosystem.
The materials keep on cycling i.e. entering the living beings and through
death and decay returning to the soil and atmosphere Such a flow of
materials between organisms and their environment is called Cycling of
materials or mineral circulation or Biogeochemical cycles (You have
learnt in class IX ).
Energy enters the producers in the ecosystem from the sun in
the form of solar energy or solar radiation. No other organisms
except green plants and Photosynthetic bacteria due to due to the
presence of chlorophyll are capable of absorbing solar energy and
converting it into chemical energy (food).
Solar energy Producers (Chemical energy) Consumers (Chemical energy)

Local Qwen — Retrieved evidence

In a food chain, the amount of energy transferred from one trophic level to the next decreases. This is because at each transfer, a large proportion (about 80 to 90 percent) of the energy is lost as heat due to processes like respiration. As a result, very little energy remains available for the top carnivores after three steps in the food chain. This energy loss explains why food chains are usually short, with not more than four steps.

Everyone is familiar with one’s own surrounding.
Our surroundings
play an important role in the survival of all organisms.
The sum of physical
and biological factors along with their chemical interactions that affect an
organism is called environment.
The living organisms always try to maintain
a balance among themselves and with biotic and abiotic factors.
All
components of biosphere interact in an organized manner with the
organisms.
This interaction assures an organism to survive that may result
in gradual evolution of the organisms in the biosphere.
The physical factors
refer to abiotic factors (land, air, water, sunlight etc.) and biological factors
refer to biotic factors (flora and fauna).
The place where an organism lives
is called habitat.
An organism can’t completely defy the balance to suit
one’s need.
It would in some way or the other affect the balance in such a
way that the survival of the organism affecting the
damage would be at stake.
You have understood the relationships between
organisms and their food in earlier classes with
the help of food chains and food webs.
Food chains
are interconnected and when we try to observe
these connections among a number of food chains
then it becomes a food web.
As you know a food
chain shows who eats what in a particular habitat.

Reflection of light at curved surfaces207 Our Environment
You quickly go through a comparable system of
ecosystems, starting with tropical rain forest at the base
and ending with perpetual snow and ice at the summit.
The main climatic influences which determine these
ecosystems are rainfall, temperature and the availability
of light from the sun.
For instance, forests are usually
associated with high rainfall, but the type of forest is
influenced by temperature and light.
The same applies
to deserts which occur in regions where rainfall is
extremely low.
But these links are never as simple or rigid as the
word ‘chain’ suggests.
For example, aphids are eaten by
many insectivorous birds in addition to warblers, and also
ladybirds and other insects; eagles, on the other hand,
prey upon a considerable variety of birds and small
mammal.
So the term food web is often a better one to use when being
precise, as it suggests a far greater number of possible links and reflects the
fact that the whole community is a complex inter-connected unit.
Thus the
original energy from the sun flows through the whole ecosystem from one
tropic level to another.
Let us observe the figure-2 which shows some of the feeding
relationships amongst organisms living in deciduous woodland.
You will
see from the diagram that animals fit into special positions within the
food web; each is described as its niche.
For instance, there is a niche for
insects such as aphids which suck up the juices of leaves.
Another niche
for insects such as caterpillars which have strong jaws for biting off pieces
of a leaf and a niche for relatively large animals such as deer which browse
on the vegetation.
All these animals feed on leaves but they differ both in
size and in the manner in which they feed.
So the term ‘niche’ denotes not
only the animal’s position in the food web and what it eats, but also its
mode of life.
Just as a habitat is the place where an animal lives, so a niche
describes its occupation the way it ‘goes about its business and earns its
livings.

9.2 Food Web
In nature food chains are usually not simple and
linear.
They are often interlinked, because at every
stage or trophic level consumers have several
alternative forms of food to choose from.
For
example, in the fig.-3 snakes prey upon frogs, mice
and small birds.
Similarly, cranes prey upon fish and
frogs.
As a result, food chains become branched and
interlinked at various stages leading to a web-like
structure.
This is called a food web.

Thus the mineral matter is constantly being removed from the earth to

curd that we eat is processed from milk, which comes from a cow, which

In every case, the origin of food materials can be traced back to green

Once the food is eaten, its energy follows a variety of pattern through

feathers, insect exoskeletons, cartilage and bone in animal foods, cellulose

materials are either ejected by defecation or regurgitated as indigested
remains.
Assimilated energy (that is not lost through respiration or excretion)
is available for the synthesis of new biomass through growth and
reproduction.
Organisms lose some biomass by death, disease or annual
leaf-drop, where they enter the detritus pathways of the food chain i.e.,
after the death and decomposition of organisms the materials flow back
into the environment(soil, water, air).
The remaining biomass is eventually
consumed by herbivores or predators and its energy there by enters the
next higher trophic level in the ecosystem.
The materials keep on cycling i.e. entering the living beings and through
death and decay returning to the soil and atmosphere Such a flow of
materials between organisms and their environment is called Cycling of
materials or mineral circulation or Biogeochemical cycles (You have
learnt in class IX ).
Energy enters the producers in the ecosystem from the sun in
the form of solar energy or solar radiation.
No other organisms
except green plants and Photosynthetic bacteria due to due to the
presence of chlorophyll are capable of absorbing solar energy and
converting it into chemical energy (food).

Reflection of light at curved surfaces213 Our Environment
From the producers, the chemical energy passes to the consumers
from one trophic level to the next through food.
At each trophic level,
organisms use most of the food energy that they assimilate into their bodies
to fulfill their metabolic requirements- performance of work, growth and
reproduction.
Because biological energy transformations are inefficient,
a substantial proportion of metabolized food energy is lost, unused as
heat.
Hence pyramid of energy is always upright.
Only a small fraction goes to the eater at next trophic level.
Organisms
are no different from man-made machines in this respect.
Most of the
energy in petrol is lost as heat in a car’s engine rather than being
transformed into the energy of motion.
In natural communities, energy
used to perform work or dissipated as heat cannot be consumed by other
organism and is forever lost to the ecosystem.

In a food chain, the amount of energy transferred from one step to the next decreases significantly. At each transfer, a large proportion of energy, about 80 to 90 percent, is lost as heat during processes like respiration. This means that only a small fraction of the energy is passed on to the next trophic level. As a result, after three steps in a food chain, very little energy is available for top carnivores to use. This is why food chains are typically short, consisting of only a few steps.

You quickly go through a comparable system of
ecosystems, starting with tropical rain forest at the base
and ending with perpetual snow and ice at the summit.
The main climatic influences which determine these
ecosystems are rainfall, temperature and the availability
of light from the sun.
For instance, forests are usually
associated with high rainfall, but the type of forest is
influenced by temperature and light.
The same applies
to deserts which occur in regions where rainfall is
extremely low.
But these links are never as simple or rigid as the
word ‘chain’ suggests.
For example, aphids are eaten by
many insectivorous birds in addition to warblers, and also
ladybirds and other insects; eagles, on the other hand,
prey upon a considerable variety of birds and small
mammal.
So the term food web is often a better one to use when being
precise, as it suggests a far greater number of possible links and reflects the
fact that the whole community is a complex inter-connected unit.
Thus the
original energy from the sun flows through the whole ecosystem from one
tropic level to another.
Let us observe the figure-2 which shows some of the feeding
relationships amongst organisms living in deciduous woodland.
You will
see from the diagram that animals fit into special positions within the
food web; each is described as its niche.
For instance, there is a niche for
insects such as aphids which suck up the juices of leaves.
Another niche
for insects such as caterpillars which have strong jaws for biting off pieces
of a leaf and a niche for relatively large animals such as deer which browse
on the vegetation.
All these animals feed on leaves but they differ both in
size and in the manner in which they feed.
So the term ‘niche’ denotes not
only the animal’s position in the food web and what it eats, but also its
mode of life.
Just as a habitat is the place where an animal lives, so a niche
describes its occupation the way it ‘goes about its business and earns its
livings.

In nature food chains are usually not simple and
linear.
They are often interlinked, because at every
stage or trophic level consumers have several
alternative forms of food to choose from.
For

and small birds.
Similarly, cranes prey upon fish and
frogs.
As a result, food chains become branched and
interlinked at various stages leading to a web-like
structure.
This is called a food web.

How does the use of toxic materials affect an ecosystem? Explain bioaccumulation and biomagnification.

Required answer points

  • Persistent toxic substances enter organisms/food chains
  • Bioaccumulation is pollutant build-up in an organism or entry into a food chain
  • Biomagnification is increasing concentration across trophic levels
  • Top consumers can receive harmful concentrations
  • Toxins can disrupt food chains and ecosystem balance

Optional answer points

  • Give pesticides or heavy metals as examples

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • Biodegradable pollutants always biomagnify indefinitely

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

The use of toxic materials, such as pesticides, herbicides, and fungicides, can have harmful effects on an ecosystem. These toxic substances can enter the environment through soil, water, and air, and they can affect both plants and animals. When these toxic materials are used in large quantities, they can cause a variety of problems, including the death of beneficial organisms like predators that control pest populations. This can lead to an imbalance in the ecosystem, as the food chain is disrupted.

When a forest is cut down and a food crop is grown in its place, a
natural established ecosystem with its vast number of species in a state of
dynamic equilibrium is replaced by a monoculture. It is an unnatural
concentration of a single crop of various kinds grown in different fields
to provide cereals and grass for domestic animals.
When we grow crops in large concentrations we also get food in
abundant quantities. This situation is optimum for pest, parasites like fungi
to grow on this food material. If the quantities of food are larger then
multiplication of pests and parasites is rapid and the resulting damage would
be great. To avoid such happening we have tried to eliminate these
competitors for the crops by using toxic chemicals (pesticides, herbicides,
and fungicides). Many of them have been very effective, but their use has
also created new problems.
The perfect pesticide is the one which destroys a particular pest and is
completely harmless to each and every other form of life, no such pesticide
exists or likely to be.
x Name any two pesticides/insecticides you have heard about.
x How are the food grains and cereals being stored in your house
and how do you protected them from pests and fungus?
Pesticides are often indiscriminate in their action and vast number of
other animals may be destroyed. Some of these may be predators which
naturally feed on these pests, others may be the prey for other animals.
Thus causing unpredictable changes in food chains and upsetting the balance
within the ecosystem. When these get mixed up in the soil the effect they
cause is even more dangerous.
Pesticides vary in their length of “life” as toxic substances. Some of
the pesticides as well as herbicides are degradable. They are broken down
into harmless substances in a comparatively short time, usually a year.
Others are non degradable, and include those which contain mercury,
arsenic or lead. These non degradable pesticides are potentially dangerous
as they accumulate in the bodies of animals and pass right through food
web. Being further concentrated at each step until animals at the top of
pyramid may receive enough to do considerable harm. The process of entry
of pollutants into a food chain is known as Bioaccumulation, whereas the
tendency of pollutants to concentrate as they move from one trophic level
to the next is known as Biomagnification.

bioaccumulation on human health.

gold

The use of toxic materials, such as pesticides and herbicides, can significantly affect an ecosystem. These substances are often used to eliminate pests and protect crops, but they can also harm other organisms within the ecosystem. Pesticides are not selective and can destroy a wide range of animals, including those that are natural predators of pests. This disruption can lead to unpredictable changes in food chains and upset the ecological balance. Two important processes related to the impact of toxic materials are bioaccumulation and biomagnification. Bioaccumulation refers to the entry and buildup of pollutants in the tissues of organisms over time. When these pollutants are not easily broken down, they accumulate in the bodies of animals. Biomagnification, on the other hand, describes how these pollutants become more concentrated as they move up the food chain. As a result, animals at higher trophic levels, such as top predators, can accumulate harmful levels of toxins, which can lead to significant health issues or even death. These processes highlight the dangers of using non-degradable toxic substances, as they can persist in the environment and cause long-term ecological harm.

Local Qwen — Retrieved evidence

The use of toxic materials, such as pesticides, can have harmful effects on an ecosystem. These materials can enter the food chain through various ways, such as being absorbed by plants or water, and then consumed by animals. This process is known as bioaccumulation, where toxic substances accumulate in the bodies of organisms over time. As these toxins move up the food chain, their concentration increases at each level, a process called biomagnification. This means that top-level consumers, such as large fish or birds of prey, end up with the highest concentrations of toxins, which can lead to serious health problems or even death. The use of toxic materials can disrupt the balance of an ecosystem, harm wildlife, and affect human health as well.

9.6.1 Biological Principles
The long term solution to this problem is to find other effective
methods of controlling pests which have far less harmful effects and are
based on sound biological principles.
Here are some of the important methods to be used.
Rotation of crops: Growing different crops on a particular piece of land
in successive years reduces the occurence of pests and damage to the
crops from year to year in that area.
Studying the life histories of the pests: By understanding how the pests
spread and its stages in life history, the seeds can be sown at that time to
reduce the damage to the crop.
Biological control: Introducing natural predators or parasites of the pests.
Genetic strains: The development of genetic strains (genetically modified
plants) which are resistant to certain pest.
Environmental ethics: This is concerned with morality of human activities
as they affect the environment.

The use of toxic materials, such as pesticides and industrial chemicals, can have significant effects on ecosystems. These substances can enter the environment through various means, such as agricultural runoff or industrial discharges, and can lead to pollution of water bodies and soil. One of the key processes affected by toxic materials is bioaccumulation. Bioaccumulation refers to the entry and buildup of pollutants in the tissues of organisms. When these pollutants enter a food chain, they can become more concentrated at each successive trophic level, a process known as biomagnification. This means that top predators, such as hawks or large fish, can accumulate high levels of toxins, which can be harmful or even lethal. For example, if a pesticide is used on crops, it may wash into nearby water bodies, affecting aquatic life. Small organisms like plankton may absorb the pesticide, and when fish eat the plankton, they accumulate more of the toxin. As larger fish eat the smaller ones, the concentration of the toxin increases further. This can lead to health problems for animals at the top of the food chain, including humans who consume these fish. Thus, the use of toxic materials can disrupt food chains and food webs, leading to a decrease in biodiversity and affecting the balance of ecosystems.

When a forest is cut down and a food crop is grown in its place, a
natural established ecosystem with its vast number of species in a state of
dynamic equilibrium is replaced by a monoculture.
It is an unnatural
concentration of a single crop of various kinds grown in different fields
to provide cereals and grass for domestic animals.
When we grow crops in large concentrations we also get food in
abundant quantities.
This situation is optimum for pest, parasites like fungi
to grow on this food material.
If the quantities of food are larger then
multiplication of pests and parasites is rapid and the resulting damage would
be great.
To avoid such happening we have tried to eliminate these
competitors for the crops by using toxic chemicals (pesticides, herbicides,
and fungicides).
Many of them have been very effective, but their use has
also created new problems.
The perfect pesticide is the one which destroys a particular pest and is
completely harmless to each and every other form of life, no such pesticide
exists or likely to be.
x Name any two pesticides/insecticides you have heard about.
x How are the food grains and cereals being stored in your house
and how do you protected them from pests and fungus?
Pesticides are often indiscriminate in their action and vast number of
other animals may be destroyed.
Some of these may be predators which
naturally feed on these pests, others may be the prey for other animals.
Thus causing unpredictable changes in food chains and upsetting the balance
within the ecosystem.
When these get mixed up in the soil the effect they
cause is even more dangerous.
Pesticides vary in their length of “life” as toxic substances.
Some of
the pesticides as well as herbicides are degradable.
They are broken down
into harmless substances in a comparatively short time, usually a year.
Others are non degradable, and include those which contain mercury,
arsenic or lead.
These non degradable pesticides are potentially dangerous
as they accumulate in the bodies of animals and pass right through food
web.
Being further concentrated at each step until animals at the top of
pyramid may receive enough to do considerable harm.
The process of entry
of pollutants into a food chain is known as Bioaccumulation, whereas the
tendency of pollutants to concentrate as they move from one trophic level
to the next is known as Biomagnification.

9.6.1 Biological Principles
The long term solution to this problem is to find other effective
methods of controlling pests which have far less harmful effects and are
based on sound biological principles.
Here are some of the important methods to be used.
Rotation of crops: Growing different crops on a particular piece of land
in successive years reduces the occurence of pests and damage to the
crops from year to year in that area.
Studying the life histories of the pests: By understanding how the pests
spread and its stages in life history, the seeds can be sown at that time to
reduce the damage to the crop.
Biological control: Introducing natural predators or parasites of the pests.
Genetic strains: The development of genetic strains (genetically modified
plants) which are resistant to certain pest.
Environmental ethics: This is concerned with morality of human activities
as they affect the environment.
People need to know besides laws regarding
environment there are some basic ethics what is right and what is wrong in
view of environment.
So one should have awareness about our environment.

19 GEN-BIO-019

What is sustainable development? How is it useful in natural resource management?

Required answer points

  • Define sustainable development as using the environment while retaining resources for the future
  • Connect development with conservation
  • Explain management/conservation of renewable and non-renewable resources

Optional answer points

  • Give a local water, forest, soil, or energy example

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • Sustainability means prohibiting all resource use

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

Sustainable development refers to using the environment in ways that ensure we have resources for the future. It is useful in natural resource management because it helps us manage and conserve resources in a way that meets our current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Sustainable development ensures that resources like forests are preserved for long-term use, preventing their destruction due to overexploitation. For example, sustainable forestry practices help maintain forests as renewable resources, supporting biodiversity, reducing soil erosion, and mitigating climate change by preventing the release of greenhouse gases.

10.4 Forest: an important renewable resource
x Why do you think forests are very important?
Every continent except Antarctica has forests. Forests are habitat for
flora and fauna. Forests serve as a lung for the world and a bed of nutrients
for new life to prosper. They provide us innumerable products and in an
urge to extract them we indiscriminately destroy them.
People clear forests to use the wood, or to make way for farming or
development. Each year, the Earth loses about 36 million acres of forest
to deforestation.
Deforestation destroys wildlife habitats and increases soil erosion. It
results the release of gases like CO, CO2, SO2 (also called as green house
gases) into the atmosphere, contributing to global warming.
Sustainable forestry practices are critical for ensuring resources well
into the future. Perhaps the bishnoi’s of Rajasthan could tell us how. As
we recall brave Amrita Devi and her daughters, followed by villagers who
clung to trees in the forest surrounding their village and laid down their
lives to save them, we are faced with a realization about how great a
movement towards conservation can be. They were protesting against the
Kings’ order to collect wood for the construction of his palace and
defending the pledge of peaceful coexistence taken by them as a bishnoi.
It is a set of 29 rules to conserve natures’ resources that every bishnoi
vows to protect.

GPT-4o API — Gold evidence

gold

Sustainable development is the practice of using the environment in ways that ensure resources are available for the future. It involves managing and conserving resources so that development and conservation can coexist harmoniously. This approach is crucial in natural resource management because it helps maintain the balance of ecosystems while allowing for human needs to be met. For example, sustainable forestry practices ensure that forests continue to provide resources and habitats without being depleted. This is important because forests are vital for biodiversity, climate regulation, and providing resources like wood and food. By adopting sustainable practices, we can prevent issues like deforestation, which leads to habitat destruction and contributes to global warming through the release of greenhouse gases.

10.3 Natural resources around us
The Earth’s natural resources include air, water, soil, minerals, fuels,
plants, and animals.
Conservation is the practice of caring for these
resources so all living things can benefit from them now and in the future.
All the things we need to survive, such as food, water, air, and shelter,
come from natural resources.
Some of these resources can be replaced
after they are used and are called renewable resources.
Other resources,
such as fossil fuels, cannot be replaced at all.
Once they are used up, they
are gone forever.

This is because it takes a long time for their formation while their

People often waste natural resources.
Animals are overhunted.
Forests
are cleared, exposing land to wind and water damage.
Fertile soil is

supplies are depleted.

If resources are carelessly managed, many will be used up.
If used

Through conservation, people can reduce waste and manage natural
resources wisely.
The population of human beings has grown enormously in the past
two centuries.
Billions of people use up resources quickly as they eat
food, build houses, produce goods and burn fuel for transportation and
electricity.
The continuation of life as we know depends on the careful
use of natural resources.
The need to conserve resources often conflicts with other
needs.
For some people, a forest area may be a good place to put
a farm.
A timber company may want to harvest the area’s trees for
construction materials.
A business company may want to build a
factory or shopping mall on the land.
All these needs are valid for
us, but sometimes the plants and animals that live in the area are
forgotten.
The benefits of development need to be weighed against
the harm to animals that may be forced to find new habitats, the
depletion of resources we may want in the future (such as water
or timber), or damage to resources we use today.

Some sustainable forestry methods include harvesting with natural
regeneration in mind, and avoiding certain logging techniques, such as
removing all the high-value trees or all the large trees from a forest.
Trees can also be conserved if consumers recycle some forest
products.
People in China and Mexico, for example, reuse much of their
wastepaper, including writing paper, wrapping paper, and cardboard.
If half
the world’s paper were recycled, much of the worldwide demand for new
paper would be fulfilled, saving many trees.
10.5 Soil
Soil is vital to food production.
We need high-quality soil to grow the
crops that we need.
Soil is also important to plants that grow in the wild.
Many other types of conservation efforts, such as plant conservation and
E3 X Biology EM 2025-26.pdf · pdf p.251 · book p.242 · rank 3 · chunk biology:fixed:00154
areas should be set aside as parks and wildlife preserves.
Governments
also enforce laws designed to protect the environment from pollution,
such as requiring factories to install pollution-control devices.
Finally,
governments often provide incentives for conserving resources.
Many international organizations are also dedicated to conservation.
Members support causes such as saving rain forests, protecting threatened
animals, and cleaning up the air.
The International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) is an
alliance of governments and private groups founded in 1948.
The IUCN
works to protect wildlife and habitats.
In 1980, the group proposed a world
conservation strategy.
Many governments have used the IUCN model to
develop their own conservation plans.
In addition, the IUCN monitors the
status of endangered wildlife, threatened national parks and preserves, and
other environments around the world.

Sustainable development is the practice of using resources in a way that ensures they are available for future generations. It involves balancing the need for development with the need to conserve natural resources and protect the environment. This approach allows us to meet our current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. In natural resource management, sustainable development is crucial because it helps ensure that resources like water, soil, and forests are used efficiently and responsibly. By managing these resources sustainably, we can prevent their depletion and maintain ecological balance. For example, sustainable forestry practices ensure that trees are harvested in a way that allows forests to regenerate, preserving habitats for wildlife and maintaining biodiversity.

10.3 Natural resources around us
The Earth’s natural resources include air, water, soil, minerals, fuels,
plants, and animals.
Conservation is the practice of caring for these
resources so all living things can benefit from them now and in the future.
All the things we need to survive, such as food, water, air, and shelter,
come from natural resources.
Some of these resources can be replaced
after they are used and are called renewable resources.
Other resources,
such as fossil fuels, cannot be replaced at all.
Once they are used up, they
are gone forever.

This is because it takes a long time for their formation while their
consumption occurs very quickly.
These are non renewable resources.
People often waste natural resources.
Animals are overhunted.
Forests
are cleared, exposing land to wind and water damage.
Fertile soil is
exhausted and lost to erosion because of poor farming practices.
Fuel
supplies are depleted.
Water and air are polluted.
If resources are carelessly managed, many will be used up.
If used
wisely and efficiently, however, renewable resources will last much longer.
Through conservation, people can reduce waste and manage natural
resources wisely.
The population of human beings has grown enormously in the past
two centuries.
Billions of people use up resources quickly as they eat
food, build houses, produce goods and burn fuel for transportation and
electricity.
The continuation of life as we know depends on the careful
use of natural resources.
The need to conserve resources often conflicts with other
needs.
For some people, a forest area may be a good place to put
a farm.
A timber company may want to harvest the area’s trees for
construction materials.
A business company may want to build a
factory or shopping mall on the land.
All these needs are valid for
us, but sometimes the plants and animals that live in the area are
forgotten.
The benefits of development need to be weighed against
the harm to animals that may be forced to find new habitats, the
depletion of resources we may want in the future (such as water
or timber), or damage to resources we use today.

10.4 Forest: an important renewable resource
x Why do you think forests are very important?
Every continent except Antarctica has forests.
Forests are habitat for
flora and fauna.
Forests serve as a lung for the world and a bed of nutrients
for new life to prosper.
They provide us innumerable products and in an
urge to extract them we indiscriminately destroy them.
People clear forests to use the wood, or to make way for farming or
development.
Each year, the Earth loses about 36 million acres of forest
to deforestation.
Deforestation destroys wildlife habitats and increases soil erosion.
It
results the release of gases like CO, CO2, SO2 (also called as green house
gases) into the atmosphere, contributing to global warming.
Sustainable forestry practices are critical for ensuring resources well
into the future.
Perhaps the bishnoi’s of Rajasthan could tell us how.
As
we recall brave Amrita Devi and her daughters, followed by villagers who
clung to trees in the forest surrounding their village and laid down their
lives to save them, we are faced with a realization about how great a
movement towards conservation can be.
They were protesting against the
Kings’ order to collect wood for the construction of his palace and
defending the pledge of peaceful coexistence taken by them as a bishnoi.
It is a set of 29 rules to conserve natures’ resources that every bishnoi
vows to protect.
Reflection of light at curved surfaces237 Natural Resources
You have studied about the Chenchu and Gond tribes of our state and
are aware of how carefully they extract resources from nature and help
revive it. (refer lesson of VII class - Forest our life)
Some sustainable forestry methods include harvesting with natural
regeneration in mind, and avoiding certain logging techniques, such as
removing all the high-value trees or all the large trees from a forest.
Trees can also be conserved if consumers recycle some forest
products.
People in China and Mexico, for example, reuse much of their
wastepaper, including writing paper, wrapping paper, and cardboard.
If half
the world’s paper were recycled, much of the worldwide demand for new
paper would be fulfilled, saving many trees.
10.5 Soil
Soil is vital to food production.
We need high-quality soil to grow the
crops that we need.
Soil is also important to plants that grow in the wild.
Many other types of conservation efforts, such as plant conservation and
E3 X Biology EM 2025-26.pdf · pdf p.251 · book p.242 · rank 3 · chunk biology:fixed:00154
areas should be set aside as parks and wildlife preserves.
Governments
also enforce laws designed to protect the environment from pollution,
such as requiring factories to install pollution-control devices.
Finally,
governments often provide incentives for conserving resources.
Many international organizations are also dedicated to conservation.
Members support causes such as saving rain forests, protecting threatened
animals, and cleaning up the air.
The International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) is an
alliance of governments and private groups founded in 1948.
The IUCN
works to protect wildlife and habitats.
In 1980, the group proposed a world
conservation strategy.
Many governments have used the IUCN model to
develop their own conservation plans.
In addition, the IUCN monitors the
status of endangered wildlife, threatened national parks and preserves, and
other environments around the world.

Why is it important to recharge the ground water sources?

Required answer points

  • Groundwater is heavily used and can be depleted by over-extraction
  • Recharge stores rainwater underground and revives dried wells
  • Recharge supports irrigation and future water availability
  • Name textbook measures such as dykes/barriers, percolation/storage structures, or field bunds

Optional answer points

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

Recharging groundwater sources is important because it helps maintain a steady supply of fresh water for various uses, including agriculture and daily life. Groundwater is a crucial source of fresh water, making up about 0.7–0.8% of the total freshwater on Earth. If groundwater sources are not recharged, they can become depleted, leading to water scarcity. The textbook explains that recharging dried-up wells helps farmers, as seen in the case study of V addicherla, where farmers were able to restore their groundwater resources by building dykes or barriers in nearby canals to retain rainwater. This practice ensures that water is available for irrigation and other essential needs, supporting agricultural productivity and the livelihoods of farmers.

come from natural resources.

after they are used and are called renewable resources.

such as fossil fuels, cannot be replaced at all.

21 GEN-PSC-001

Why do we prefer a convex mirror as a rear-view mirror in the vehicles?

Required answer points

  • A convex mirror forms a virtual, erect, diminished image
  • It provides a wider field of view
  • Therefore a driver can see a larger region behind the vehicle

Optional answer points

  • Image properties hold for different object positions

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • A convex rear-view mirror forms a real image on a screen

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

We prefer a convex mirror as a rear-view mirror in vehicles because it provides a wider field of view compared to a plane mirror. This is due to the way light reflects off a convex surface. When light rays from an object strike a convex mirror, they diverge (spread out) after reflection. This divergence allows the mirror to capture a larger area behind the vehicle, making it easier for the driver to see more of the surroundings. Additionally, the image formed by a convex mirror is always virtual, upright, and smaller than the actual object, which helps in reducing the risk of blind spots.

1.3 Ray Diagrams: (Image formation by convex mirror)
One can draw ray diagrams for a convex mirror too. The ‘easy’ rays
that we identified earlier can be used in this case with small modification.
Here there are three rules which describe these rays. The procedure for
drawing the diagram is similar and is not repeated here.
Rule 1: A ray parallel to the axis, on meeting the
convex mirror will get reflected so as to appear as if it
is coming from the focal point. See fig.-17.
Rule 2: This is
converse of Rule 1. A
ray travelling in the
direction of the focal point, after
reflection, will become parallel to the
axis. See fig.-18.
Rule 3: A ray travelling in the direction of the
centre of curvature will, on reflection, travel in the
opposite direction and appears to be coming from the
centre of curvature. See fig.-19.
Now let us use these rules to show the formation
of images when the object is placed at different places infront of the convex
mirror (see fig.-20)
AB is the object placed at any point
on the principal axis infront of the
convex mirror. Using Rule (1) and
Rule (3), we get an erected, diminished,
and virtual image between P and F on
the back side of the mirror. This image
can not be caught on screen and visible
only in the mirror. Hence this is a
virtual image. V erify this with an experiment.
Using these rules, draw ray diagrams to show formation of images
when an object is placed at different positions and note down your
conclusions. V erify your results experimentally.

We prefer a convex mirror as a rear-view mirror in vehicles because it forms an erected, diminished, and virtual image of objects. This means that the image is smaller than the actual object, allowing the driver to see a wider field of view. This is particularly useful for seeing more of the road and traffic behind the vehicle, enhancing safety while driving. Local Qwen — Retrieved evidence

We prefer a convex mirror as a rear-view mirror in vehicles because it provides a wider field of view compared to a concave mirror. When parallel rays of light fall on a convex mirror, they appear to diverge after reflection. By extending these reflected rays backwards, they seem to meet at a point called the focus. This property of convex mirrors allows them to form virtual, erect, and diminished images of objects behind the mirror. As a result, convex mirrors help drivers see a larger area behind the vehicle, which enhances safety.

consider a ray that comes from the tip and goes in such a direction that it

1.3 Ray Diagrams: (Image formation by convex mirror)
One can draw ray diagrams for a convex mirror too.
The ‘easy’ rays
that we identified earlier can be used in this case with small modification.
Here there are three rules which describe these rays.
The procedure for
drawing the diagram is similar and is not repeated here.
Rule 1: A ray parallel to the axis, on meeting the
convex mirror will get reflected so as to appear as if it
is coming from the focal point.
See fig.-17.
Rule 2: This is
converse of Rule 1.
A
ray travelling in the
direction of the focal point, after
reflection, will become parallel to the
axis.
See fig.-18.
Rule 3: A ray travelling in the direction of the
centre of curvature will, on reflection, travel in the
opposite direction and appears to be coming from the
centre of curvature.
See fig.-19.
Now let us use these rules to show the formation
of images when the object is placed at different places infront of the convex
mirror (see fig.-20)
AB is the object placed at any point
on the principal axis infront of the
convex mirror.
Using Rule (1) and
Rule (3), we get an erected, diminished,
and virtual image between P and F on
the back side of the mirror.
This image
can not be caught on screen and visible
only in the mirror.
Hence this is a
virtual image.

retrieved

Convex mirrors are preferred as rear-view mirrors in vehicles because they provide a wider field of view compared to other types of mirrors. This is due to the way convex mirrors reflect light. When parallel rays of light hit a convex mirror, they diverge after reflection, making it appear as if they are coming from a focal point behind the mirror. This property allows drivers to see a larger area of the road behind them, which is crucial for safety while driving. Additionally, the images formed by convex mirrors are diminished, meaning they appear smaller, which helps in fitting a larger scene into the mirror view. These images are also virtual and erect, making them easy to interpret for the driver.

22 GEN-PSC-002

Find the distance of the image, when an object is placed on the principal axis, at a distance of 10 cm in front of a concave mirror whose radius of curvature is 8 cm.

Required answer points

  • Use f = R/2 = -4 cm and u = -10 cm under the textbook sign convention
  • Apply 1/f = 1/v + 1/u
  • Obtain v = -20/3 cm ≈ -6.67 cm
  • Interpret the negative sign as a real image on the object side

Optional answer points

  • The image is inverted and diminished between F and C

Prohibited / unsupported claims

  • Report v as +6.7 cm while also calling it a real same-side image

Local Qwen — Gold evidence

To find the distance of the image formed by a concave mirror, we use the mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u. Here, the object distance (u) is given as -10 cm (negative because the object is placed in front of the mirror). The radius of curvature (R) is given as 8 cm, so the focal length (f) is half of the radius of curvature, which is 4 cm. Substituting these values into the mirror formula, we get 1/4 = 1/v + 1/(-10). Solving this equation, we find that the image distance (v) is -40/3 cm or approximately -13.33 cm. The negative sign indicates that the image is formed in front of the mirror, which means it is a real image.

GPT-4o API — Gold evidence

gold

To find the distance of the image when an object is placed on the principal axis of a concave mirror, we can use the mirror formula: \[ \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} \] where: - \( f \) is the focal length of the mirror, - \( v \) is the image distance, - \( u \) is the object distance. Given: - Object distance \( u = -10 \) cm (the negative sign indicates that the object is in front of the mirror), - Radius of curvature \( R = 8 \) cm. The focal length \( f \) is half of the radius of curvature: \[ f = \frac{R}{2} = \frac{8}{2} = 4 \text{ cm} \] Substitute the values into the mirror formula: \[ \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{-10} \] Solving for \( \frac{1}{v} \): \[ \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{10} \] \[ \frac{1}{v} = \frac{5}{20} + \frac{2}{20} = \frac{7}{20} \] Thus, \( v = \frac{20}{7} \approx 2.86 \text{ cm} \). Therefore, the image distance is approximately 2.86 cm in front of the mirror.

Local Qwen — Retrieved evidence

To find the distance of the image formed by a concave mirror, we use the mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u. Here, the object is placed at a distance of 10 cm in front of the mirror, so u = -10 cm (negative because the object is on the same side as the incoming light). The radius of curvature (R) is given as 8 cm, so the focal length (f) is half of the radius of curvature, which is f = R/2 = 8/2 = 4 cm. Since it is a concave mirror, the focal length is negative, so f = -4 cm. Substituting these values into the mirror formula: 1/(-4) = 1/v + 1/(-10). Solving this equation gives 1/v = 1/(-4) - 1/(-10) = -1/4 + 1/10 = -5/20 + 2/20 = -3/20. Therefore, v = -20/3 ≈ -6.67 cm. The negative sign indicates that the image is formed on the same side as the object, which is the real image.
